value.text: Cleanup crews and residents are continuing to clear damage left behind by an EF-1 tornado that tore through southern Palm Beach County on Saturday evening, toppling trees and damaging homes, vehicles and other property from west Boca Raton through west Delray Beach.WATCH: EF-1 tornado cleanup continues in Delray BeachThe National Weather Service said the tornado reached peak winds of 102 mph and traveled 7.64 miles after first touching down around 6:04 p.m. near Boca Gardens. It remained on the ground until about 6:31 p.m., ending southwest of Boynton Beach. No deaths or injuries were reported. WPTV crews surveying damage in the Delray Beach area found a massive tree that came crashing down and crushed a stone wall. Landscaping crews said they have been clearing damaged and fallen trees since Sunday.Tony Symia lives in an apartment just feet from where the tornado passed.He told WPTV the storm announced itself with a sound he had never experienced before."Well, we heard it was like a train coming through," Symia said. "It was pretty rumbling when it came through, and I rushed my wife into the bathroom, and it only lasted about a minute."Symia said he had never experienced a tornado before and worries he did not initially react quickly enough."I kind of think I reacted late because it all started prior to me getting her into the bathroom," he said.When Symia stepped outside the following morning, he could see just how much had changed around his home."The tree was coming through there, and it ended up over here," he said. "You couldn't get through here. You had to drive around, and there was another two or three trees down here."The damage was widespread along the tornado's path. The National Weather Service reported extensive tree damage and some roof damage, while WPTV found uprooted trees, damaged homes and vehicles crushed by falling trees in communities across western Boca Raton and Delray Beach.In Boca Gardens, WPTV documented an uprooted tree that lifted concrete in a parking lot before landing on three parked vehicles. Landscaping and cleanup crews have been working since Sunday to remove fallen trees and debris."We've been picking up the damaged trees since Sunday," one landscaper told WPTV in Spanish.While the physical evidence of the tornado is slowly being hauled away, Symia said the sound of the storm remains difficult to forget."We heard a rumble," he recalled.For a resident who had never before experienced a tornado, what stands out most is how quickly that rumble became a dangerous storm."It happened so fast," Symia said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

St. Lucie County commissioners are scheduled to consider adopting the final draft of the 2026 Port of Fort Pierce Master Plan during their Dec. 1 meeting. County Port, Inlet and Beaches staff will present the plan at the meeting, which begins at 6 p.m. Commissioners can ask questions and approve the document as presented or amend it before adoption, according to the county. The update builds on the port’s 2020 master plan and incorporates feedback from residents and industry stakeholders since commissioners last reviewed the draft on Aug. 11. The plan is intended to guide future development and help the county seek state and federal grants for port improvements. Among the long-term opportunities in the draft is a Launch Vehicle Recovery Facility to support offshore rocket recovery operations, including drone ships and other support vessels. As CBS12 previously reported, the proposed facility could position Fort Pierce to support recovery work tied to Florida’s growing space industry . The plan describes it as one part of a broader working waterfront vision, alongside mega-yacht services, marine research and workforce training, recreation and public access. The rocket-recovery proposal is one part of a broader vision for the Port of Fort Pierce as a mixed-use working waterfront. The plan also outlines Harbour Pointe as a public-facing district, with a regional boat ramp, waterfront dining and commercial space, an entertainment pavilion, a shared-use path and a living shoreline. The update also envisions a marine research and workforce training campus focused on marine science, environmental education and training for waterfront jobs. It calls for continued growth of the port’s mega-yacht maintenance and repair operations, as well as a marina at Museum Pointe where yachts could dock temporarily for crew changes, provisioning or staging before service. The plan includes infrastructure and access projects, such as a new road to Harbour Pointe, stormwater improvements and a possible connection to the regional Sun Trail. It also proposes a future Port to Park link to improve access between the waterfront and Franklin Park. See also: 3 auto insurers directed to refund $122 million in excess profits to Florida customers The 2026 update supplements the port’s 2020 master plan rather than replacing it. The document lays out a long-term vision for development; proposed zoning changes and the Port Overlay District remain under discussion. The county says commissioners will consider the plan during their regular meeting in the Commission Chambers on the third floor of the Roger Poitras Administration Annex, 2300 Virginia Ave. in Fort Pierce. The meeting will also be streamed on the county’s website and YouTube channel. Residents can review the draft plan on the county’s Port Master Plan webpage .

An EF-1 tornado that swept through southern Palm Beach County over the weekend left residents in the Boca Gardens community of west Boca Raton cleaning up downed trees and damaged property, including a car crushed by a massive tree.Two days after the tornado, cleanup crews were still working through Boca Gardens, where residents described powerful winds, widespread debris and the shock of seeing the damage once the storm had passed.WATCH: West Boca Raton neighbors clean up EF-1 tornado damageBoca Gardens residents describe tornado's impactGreg Ciaro and Angela Cairo live yards from where a large tree came down. The couple told WPTV they realized afterward how much worse the damage could have been."The wind just came down, really strong," Greg said."Total devastation. I mean, we walked out afterward, and you're just in shock," Angela said.The family said the tree's proximity to their home made clear how narrowly they avoided more serious damage."I mean, if you think about it, it's literally right there. So any shift this way easily could've been much, much worse," he said.Tree crushes neighbor's carDown the road, resident Alvaro Villa Correa is dealing with the loss of his vehicle after a tree came crashing down on it."The car is a total loss. It's too badly damaged," Villa Correa told WPTV. "The roof, the hood, the trunk, there's major damage."Cleanup crews continued cutting and removing downed trees Monday. Crews told WPTV the cleanup is expected to be a lengthy process.How El Niño can influence South Florida weatherThe tornado is one of several tornado events WPTV has reported across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast in recent years.WPTV First Alert Meteorologist Skylar Spinler said El Niño can influence local weather patterns because Pacific Ocean temperatures affect the position and strength of the subtropical jet stream."During El Niño winters, the subtropical jet stream typically strengthens and shifts further south, so think of this jet stream as a highway for storm systems," Spinler said.Neighbors thankful after close callFor residents continuing to clean up in Boca Gardens, the destruction is also a reminder of what did not happen."We were blessed. 100% we were blessed," Angela told WPTV.With Thanksgiving approaching, she said her family has an added reason to be grateful."And we've got a lot to be thankful for on Thanksgiving because it could've been so much worse," Angela said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

The holiday rush to the airport for Thanksgiving is underway, and passengers are paying more this year to fly.According to AAA, the average domestic round-trip flight is costing $800. That figure is up 17% from a year ago, largely because of jet fuel costs.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "We've seen increases this year anywhere between 20 and 30%," said Clint Henderson at The Points Guy website. "My fear is, the CEOs are basically getting used to these higher costs, and they've suggested that even if the cost of jet fuel drops, they may not lower prices that much."Henderson suggests that any last-minute holiday travelers should try booking a flight on the actual holiday to save some money.Also, it helps to be flexible when choosing a flight."I would have liked the 6 a.m. flight, but that was too expensive," said Karen Galitto, who was flying from West Palm Beach to Long Island on Monday.Another issue facing passengers is delays.Recently, computer and operational issues caused travel trouble, including this month's national ground stop and Sunday's issue that impacted Delta's weight and balance system."The reason they're delaying and canceling flights is out of an abundance of caution," Henderson said. "I wouldn't worry too much about it, but I would have a Plan B in mind," he said. "I would document any expenses you incurred during issues while you're traveling, because then you can ask potentially for compensation."

Three weeks after historic flooding damaged and destroyed homes in Riviera Beach's Lone Pine community, residents are still gutting houses, searching for materials and relying on volunteers as they try to rebuild. Now, Mayor Douglas Lawson says the city is launching Rebuild Lone Pine Together, a community-driven initiative aimed at getting money, manpower and other resources to families who need help immediately.WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman was in Lone Pine the night of the flooding and returned to the neighborhood weeks later.WATCH: Riviera Beach launches effort to rebuild Lone PineThe water is gone, but signs of the destruction remain throughout the community. Dumpsters line streets outside gutted homes as families work to rebuild their lives heading into the holiday season.Inside one of those damaged homes, Hoffman met Edward Carr.Carr doesn't live in Lone Pine. He answered a call for volunteers after historic rainfall devastated the neighborhood."They said they needed some drywall, like replaced because they had flooding," Carr said. "So as you can see, I started pulling off the baseboards."The family living in the home invited WPTV inside but asked to remain anonymous.That's also where Hoffman met Denise Smith, another Lone Pine resident."We need a lot of hands because many hands make light work," Smith said. "It's what my grandmother used to say."Smith's own home down the street was destroyed by the flooding. She showed WPTV images of the damage.Despite being displaced herself, she was helping someone else rebuild.For Smith and Carr, two needs stand out across Lone Pine: volunteers and building materials."Right now is the time for Riviera Beach to come together as one community," Lawson said.Hoffman walked through Lone Pine with Lawson as they discussed what comes next for families who cannot afford to wait.Lawson said the city is working to bring together $2 million in available funding. But he also acknowledged that accessing money can involve bureaucratic hurdles, while residents need help now.That's where Rebuild Lone Pine Together comes in."It's really driven and led by the community," Lawson said. "It's focused on community advocates, leaders, nonprofits to come together with the resources, the funding, the dollars, the manpower."The effort is designed to bring together organizations, volunteers and other partners capable of filling immediate needs as residents continue working to recover.Lawson said the call for assistance goes far beyond Riviera Beach."We're calling across this country; we're saying we need support here in Riviera Beach and Lone Pine," Lawson said. "We're asking all our shareholders, all our partners, everybody just has an interest in supporting people to come provide support."Hoffman took the mayor's plan back to Smith and Carr.Smith described herself as "optimistically hopeful."But three weeks after the flooding, she also wants to see assistance reach residents faster."I'm the glass half full kind of person, but it's, you know, it's been three weeks, and I know there's a process," Smith said. "So I just hope that the wheels can start to turn a little bit faster, because people are displaced. I'm displaced, and people really don't have places to go."For families approaching the holidays with damaged homes and uncertain living arrangements, the launch of Rebuild Lone Pine Together represents another potential path toward recovery.But the work is only beginning.WPTV will continue tracking the initiative, including whether the promised resources, volunteers and funding make their way to the families still rebuilding in Lone Pine.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. New research shows Florida law enforcement agencies could earn more than $1 billion in federal funding through next year for helping the Department of Homeland Security with immigration enforcement operations — far beyond what any other state could receive for its participation.Since February 2025, every law enforcement agency in Florida is required to have a 287(g) agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The agreement allows state and local law enforcement officers to conduct immigration enforcement activities on ICE's behalf. The 287(g) program has been around for 30 years.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "(It's) basically a program that if someone came into the jail, then the jail could run their information through an immigration database and alert ICE if they had an immigration detainer or some civil immigration issue, and then ICE could come and pick them up," said Felicity Rose, vice president of research and policy at fwd.us, a bipartisan advocacy organization that focuses on immigration and criminal justice. Rose and her team have been tracking the Trump administration's use of 287(g) agreements. They recently published a report using public and leaked records to estimate how much money local law enforcement agencies are getting from ICE in exchange for participating in 287(g)."Those partnerships are both sending billions of dollars to state and local law enforcement with very little oversight," Rose said.I asked Rose for her data on each sheriff's office in our five-county viewing area. In Palm Beach County, the report estimates more than $16 million in available funding for fiscal year 2026. In Martin County, the estimate is nearly $1.8 million, along with $5.3 million in St. Lucie County, $1.7 million in Okeechobee County and $880,000 in Indian River County.PREVIOUS COVERAGE: Several local police departments are enrolled in 287(g) program"After the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act in the summer of 2025 passed, they gave $191 billion to (the U.S. Department of Homeland Security). One thing they decided to do with that was start paying people who signed up for the task force model," Rose explained.ICE breaks down its 287(g) task force payment structure on its website: initial stipends of $100,000, plus $7,500 per credentialed officer. Then, quarterly stipends of $15,000 per officer per quarter. That's on top of salary reimbursement for officers' time working immigration enforcement, plus "quarterly monetary performance awards based on the successful location of illegal aliens.""That money led to a major change in the number of agencies signing up and, very importantly, the number of arrests that they were making," Rose said.The Florida Department of Law Enforcement tracks 287(g) arrests throughout the state. Their data states that since August 2025, the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office had 361, the Okeechobee County Sheriff's Office carried out 37, Indian River County had 38 and St. Lucie County had 15. The Martin County Sheriff's Office had 1,095 287(g) arrests.The Martin County Sheriff's Office declined an interview for this story, but Sheriff John Budensiek spoke to us in December 2025 about accepting funding to help with immigration detention."I don't think our taxpayers should be taxed again. I think the federal government, if they're going to use us as a tool, should pay for their portion of that," Budensiek said.A spokeswoman for MCSO told me in a statement that "The Martin County Sheriff's Office has not conducted any recent immigration enforcement operations under the 287(g) program. Individuals without lawful immigration status who are arrested on local criminal charges in Martin County are booked into the Martin County Jail. The number of those bookings is substantially lower than the figure you cited."Mariana Blanco and her team at the Guatemalan Maya Center in Lake Worth Beach have also been tracking immigration arrests and working with the families impacted by them."When you begin monetizing these arrests, now you lose sight of the protection of the people, and that's exactly what we're seeing," Blanco said.She tells me she's noticed a change in how and where those arrests have happened in recent months in Palm Beach County."So they're not just taking the driver in the vehicle; they're taking the passengers as well," Blanco said."When (people) called to report crimes, (deputies) have been arresting them because of their — due to their immigration status," Blanco said.I asked her if the person who called to report the crime gets arrested, and she confirmed that they do.I asked Blanco whether she worries about the impact that will have on crime overall in Lake Worth."Crime has been heavily under-reported in Lake Worth and I know that because PBSO has asked us for help in ... giving a sense of security for the people to report crimes," Blanco said. "We said, well, respectfully, we don't trust you, and so how would we tell the people that they could trust you?" The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office didn't respond to my requests for comment.The fwd.us report estimates law enforcement agencies across Florida could be eligible for a total of up to $1.4 billion through fiscal year 2027 from the federal government. The report also estimates that Florida has deputized 9,021 law enforcement officers under the 287(g) task force model and conducted 15,164 arrests since January 2025.To compare, the report shows Texas, the state believed to be eligible for the second-highest payday through 287(g), is estimated to qualify for roughly $421 million through FY 2027. The state is estimated to have deputized 4,082 officers and conducted 9,138 arrests through the program (although Rose noted that Florida provides more data on 287(g) than other states).I filed public records requests with our five local sheriff's offices to see how they were spending that money, beyond reimbursement for deputies' time. Those requests are still pending.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

One person was killed and another suffered life-threatening injuries in a four-vehicle crash near Interstate 95 in Riviera Beach early Sunday morning, police said.The Riviera Beach Police Department said officers and Riviera Beach Fire Rescue responded to the intersection of West Blue Heron Boulevard and I-95 around 5:32 a.m. after the city's communications center received multiple 911 calls reporting a crash.Police said investigators determined that a 2022 Nissan Altima exited the northbound I-95 ramp and continued across the median, striking a 2021 Acura ILX that was stopped at a red light while facing west and waiting to turn onto southbound I-95.The initial impact led to a chain-reaction crash involving two other vehicles, according to police.The driver of the Acura was pronounced dead at the scene. A 26-year-old passenger had to be extricated from the vehicle and was taken to a hospital with life-threatening injuries.Police said the driver and passenger of the Nissan were also taken to a hospital with injuries that were not considered life-threatening.The names of those involved have not been released pending notification of their families.The Riviera Beach Police Department's Traffic Homicide Unit is investigating the crash. Police said criminal charges are pending.Anyone with information about the crash is asked to contact Riviera Beach police at 561-845-4123.

Nearly 1.8 million chickens will be depopulated after highly pathogenic avian influenza, commonly known as bird flu, was detected at a Cal-Maine Foods facility in Okeechobee County.Cal-Maine Foods announced Nov. 18 that the facility tested positive for highly pathogenic avian influenza, or HPAI. The company said the outbreak will lead to the depopulation of approximately 1.4 million laying hens and 360,000 pullets, representing about 2.7% of the company's total flock.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Production at the Okeechobee County facility has temporarily stopped while Cal-Maine follows protocols established by the U.S. Department of Agriculture.The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services has established a quarantine area following the detection, according to St. Lucie County government.The poultry quarantine extends from Okeechobee County into a rural portion of western St. Lucie County north of State Road 70 near the county line.People who own or care for poultry within the affected area are being advised to review the state's quarantine restrictions, which include limits on moving poultry and poultry products without FDACS authorization. Residents can check whether they are within the affected area using the state's interactive quarantine map.Cal-Maine said it is coordinating production and distribution among its other facilities in an effort to maintain its egg supply and minimize disruptions for customers.The company also said it maintains biosecurity programs at its facilities but noted that no farm is immune to HPAI. The virus remains present among wild birds, and the risk of outbreaks can increase during bird migration seasons.Health officials say the detection does not mean consumers should stop eating eggs. According to information provided by the company, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention considers the health risk from HPAI viruses to the general U.S. public to be low.The USDA also says HPAI is not transmitted through properly handled and cooked eggs. Cal-Maine said there is no known HPAI risk associated with eggs currently on the market and that no eggs have been recalled because of the outbreak.Cal-Maine said it is working with federal, state and local officials as it responds to the outbreak and works to reduce the risk of additional infections.The company said it expects to provide more information in its next quarterly report filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission and does not anticipate providing interim updates unless information is considered material.Anyone with questions about the quarantine can contact FDACS at 850-410-0900 or find additional information through its Division of Animal Industry.

If you're driving for Thanksgiving, don't wait until the last minute to make sure your car is ready for the trip.Before packing the car and hitting the road, take a few minutes to check your vehicle.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Start with the tires. Check the air pressure on all four tires, including the spare. Look for low tread, cracks or other signs of damage that could cause trouble during a long drive.Next, pop the hood and check your oil, coolant and windshield-washer fluid. Make sure everything is at the proper level before leaving home.Drivers should also check their headlights, brake lights and turn signals to make sure they're working properly.Don't forget about the battery. If your vehicle is slow to start or the battery is several years old, consider having it tested before your Thanksgiving trip.It's also a good idea to pack an emergency kit with water, a flashlight, phone charger and basic first-aid supplies.Taking a few minutes to inspect your vehicle before leaving could help prevent a breakdown and keep your Thanksgiving road trip from ending on the side of the road.

Gov. Ron DeSantis said Florida is preparing to seek additional federal disaster assistance after a second round of historic flooding inundated communities across the state, with the St. Johns River reaching record levels and hundreds of people requiring rescue.Speaking Monday in Brevard County alongside state and local emergency officials, DeSantis said parts of Cocoa Beach and surrounding communities received 15 to 20 inches of rain in recent days. Many of those areas were still recovering from severe flooding earlier this month.WATCH BELOW: Florida seeking more federal aid after historic flooding, according to DeSantisDeSantis said the St. Johns River near Cocoa reached nearly 19 feet on Saturday, surpassing the previous record by more than a foot. He warned that because the river moves slowly, flooding could take weeks or even months to fully recede."There could be more flooding that happens in the near future," DeSantis said. "The St. Johns River is a major concern just given how high it has gotten."Florida previously requested a major federal disaster declaration following the first round of flooding earlier this month. DeSantis said that request is awaiting action from the federal government.The state is now collecting damage assessments from the latest flooding and plans to submit another request for a major disaster declaration. DeSantis said the second request will cover a broader area because more counties and communities were affected by the latest rainfall.Florida Division of Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said the state could have enough damage information to move forward with the request as soon as Monday or Tuesday.DeSantis said he expects the request to warrant federal approval."It's basically just the damage assessments trying to show that there's been enough damage to justify federal intervention," DeSantis said. "And I think in this case that that has been the case."DeSantis also said individual assistance included in the state's initial request could provide some relief to residents with damaged homes, including those who did not carry flood insurance. However, he cautioned that federal assistance may not cover the full amount of a homeowner's losses.State agencies, including the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, Florida National Guard, Florida State Guard and Florida Highway Patrol, have completed nearly 500 floodwater rescues, according to DeSantis.The Florida National Guard has mobilized 421 personnel and conducted 417 welfare checks, while deploying 54 high-water vehicles across six counties.Another 173 FWC officers are deployed, along with more than 200 FHP troopers assisting flooded communities, stranded motorists and disabled vehicles.Nearly 160 Florida State Guard personnel have also been mobilized. State Guard crews have helped with "muck and gut" operations at more than 250 properties in Brevard and Okeechobee counties, removing water-damaged material from flooded homes.The state has distributed more than 22,000 boxes of water, 7,500 ready-to-eat meals, 1,200 flood cleanup buckets and 1,300 tarps to affected communities, according to Perdue.Emergency officials warned that high water remains a threat even as conditions begin to improve.Perdue said State Road 50 in Brevard County and State Road 46 in Seminole County remained underwater as of Monday."If there are any state roads or local roads that are underwater, please do not drive or walk through the water," Perdue said. "It can be very dangerous. You just can't see what's down there."The Florida Division of Emergency Management has deployed more than 10,000 feet of temporary flood barriers to protect critical infrastructure, including government buildings and lift stations in Seminole County and HCA Florida Lake Monroe Hospital in Sanford.The state has also deployed 90 pumps and 22 vacuum trucks during the response in Brevard, Broward, Indian River, Flagler, Palm Beach, St. Lucie and Volusia counties.FDOT has more than 750 personnel working on flood assessments and pumping operations across Central and South Florida, DeSantis said.A shelter remains open at the Joseph N. Davis Community Center in Melbourne.Four multi-agency resource centers have also been established across three counties, including two in Brevard County. DeSantis said more than 1,600 residents have already received assistance through the centers. The centers will be closed on Thanksgiving.Residents whose homes are uninhabitable because of flooding can also apply for the state's temporary travel trailer program through emergencyRV.org.DeSantis said state resources will remain in affected communities throughout the recovery."Our folks aren't going anywhere," DeSantis said. We're going to see through the federal assistance and make sure that people can get back on their feet."

Hundreds of Palm Beach County families are getting help putting Thanksgiving dinner on the table through SPECTRA, the nonprofit arm of the Palm Beach County Housing Authority, as community partners work to address food insecurity during the holiday season.SPECTRA recently helped distribute 300 frozen turkeys and is now preparing Thanksgiving fixings for families in South Bay, according to Naderge Alcime, ROSS coordinator with the Palm Beach County Housing Authority.WATCH REPORT BELOW:The assistance comes as the Housing Authority says more than 280 additional families are on its waiting list for help.Filling needs beyond housingSPECTRA was created to help address needs that extend beyond putting a roof over someone's head."SPECTRA is our not-for-profit arm of the Housing Authority," Chief Financial Officer Tad Fuller said. "The Housing Authority, of course, houses individuals and families within our county. SPECTRA's job is to fill in those missing middle pieces."Fuller said those needs can include food, transportation and other services for residents.For some families, food insecurity can mean making difficult choices between basic necessities."A lot of our families are having issues with having enough food in their homes, and so having to choose between paying a light bill and or paying for childcare or buying food for Thanksgiving is a tough decision," Alcime said.300 turkeys and more help for South BayAlcime said SPECTRA recently completed a giveaway of 300 frozen turkeys and is continuing its Thanksgiving efforts in South Bay."We just did a 300 turkey giveaway last week, and now we're going to be going to South Bay to our new South Bay property and handing out, uh, these lovely fixings to go along with another partner of ours that's giving ham and pies," Alcime said.GL Homes is among the community partners supporting SPECTRA's Thanksgiving efforts.Sarah Alsofrom, vice president of community relations with GL Homes, said the company provided $5,000 for turkeys along with nonperishable food for Thanksgiving meals."We've given $5000 worth of turkeys so that people can have a happy Thanksgiving and all of these great canned items, non-perishable goods, all the trimmings, and we need more help from the community to provide more," Alsofrom said.More than 280 families are still waitingThe Thanksgiving distributions are helping hundreds of families, but Palm Beach County Housing Authority Executive Director and CEO Carol Jones-Gilbert said the need continues."We have, we've served families, but we have an additional 280 families on the waitlist," Jones-Gilbert said. "We serve more than 8000 people in Palm Beach County, so there's always a need, and so we're always looking for partners to collaborate with us."The need is particularly timely during Thanksgiving week, when the cost of preparing a holiday meal can add another expense for households already balancing food, utilities, childcare and other necessities.For SPECTRA, the goal extends beyond a single Thanksgiving meal. Jones-Gilbert said community partnerships and in-kind donations can help the Housing Authority address needs outside traditional housing assistance."Our ask is we're always looking for partners for in-kind donations to help us to not make sure, to make sure we not just provide housing, but that our families thrive," Jones-Gilbert said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Riviera Beach Mayor Douglas Lawson is asking businesses, nonprofits, faith groups and volunteers to help families in Lone Pine Estates repair their homes after severe flooding earlier this month.Lawson announced the "Rebuild Lone Pine Together" initiative Monday, calling on community partners to donate building materials and supplies, provide volunteers and offer other resources to residents recovering from the flooding.WATCH BELOW: Riviera Beach weighs flood relief planHeavy rain this month flooded homes and left neighborhood streets underwater, forcing some residents from their homes, according to the city.Riviera Beach declared a state of emergency on Nov. 2 as crews worked to pump water from flooded areas and assess the damage.City officials said some families continue to deal with flood damage as they work toward returning home.WATCH BELOW: Riviera Beach residents rescued from floodwaters"These families need more than words. They need building materials, helping hands, and neighbors who will stand with them. I'm asking our community to answer that call," Lawson said in a statement.Through Rebuild Lone Pine Together, the mayor's office is seeking help from businesses, nonprofits, faith organizations, service groups and individual residents.People and organizations can assist by donating building materials and other supplies, volunteering to help with recovery efforts or providing other resources that could help affected families repair their homes.Those interested in helping can contact the Riviera Beach Mayor's Office at 561-845-4145 or the Sincere 2000 Foundation at 561-385-4469.The initiative comes as residents of Lone Pine Estates continue recovering from a month marked by significant rainfall and flooding across parts of South Florida.

More than 150 people turned out for the 14th Annual Black Chamber of Commerce Ascension Awards. The Awards recognize small minority-owned businesses and business owners who continue to help sustain Palm Beach County.WPTV Morning anchor Hollani Davis was the emcee of the annual brunch, this year held at the Wellington National Golf Club.Nearly 30 professionals and businesses in restaurant/dining, marketing, human resources, consulting services, mentoring, public relations, legal and more were honored.The 2026 Ascension Award winners are:Nonprofit/Public Sector Organization of the Year - NAACP West Palm Beach ChapterEmerging Black Business of the Year - Kitty Lundan (Pop Star Productions)Distinguished Black Business of the Year - Dr. J. Sheree (Evolve Total Health)Young Professional of the Year - Ray NelsonDicky Sykes Social Justice Advocate Award - Telsula Morgan (Partner, Lewis Longman Walker PA)The President's Award - John Carpenter (FAU Associate Director of Executive Education).This year's awards also paid tribute to Leontyne Brown. The Palm Beach County natives work included spearheading initiatives like "Pretty Girls Vote". Brown served on the Board of Directors of the Black Chamber for nearly 15 years. She is the longest-serving Board Secretary and was posthumously recognized as Secretary Emeritus through a special resolution by the Board. Brown passed away this past Spring.

The Martin County Sheriff’s Office , along with Florida Highway Patrol, are investigating a serious crash involving a vehicle and a tractor-trailer. MCSO says a serious injury crash involving a vehicle and tractor-trailer occurred on Monday at U.S. 1 at SE Hobe Terrace in Hobe Sound. Martin County Fire Rescue’s LifeStar flew one person with life-threatening injuries to St. Mary’s Medical Center, MCSO said. A second person was also injured in the crash. See also: Boynton Beach police arrest man on fentanyl, cocaine trafficking charges This is a developing story, check back for updates.

Several organizations across the Treasure Coast are offering free food distributions, grocery giveaways and prepared Thanksgiving meals this week to help residents in need ahead of the holiday. The distributions are taking place Nov. 23-26 in Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie, Indiantown and Sebastian. Participating locations include local churches, food ministries and community organizations. Available assistance includes groceries, holiday food and prepared meals, with distribution times and offerings varying by location. Some distributions will continue while supplies last. Residents are encouraged to contact individual organizations before traveling to confirm availability, eligibility requirements and distribution details. A list of participating locations, addresses and distribution times is provided below. Two men are facing felony burglary charges after allegedly breaking into a Hutchinson Island business to play video games after hours, the Martin County Sheriff's Office said. The incident occurred late Saturday into early Sunday morning at the Indian River Plantation Shopping Plaza, according to Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek. A security guard on patrol noticed something unusual and called 911. "He happens upon an individual that had the back door of a restaurant/bowling alley game room, and as he tried to confront that individual, he fled," Budensiek said. Footage from the sheriff's Air One unit showed deputies tracking a suspect from above. "He should be coming up on your right side. Stop, stop the car," a deputy said in the video. Deputies located one man walking down the road and another emerging from the woods with an electric scooter. "Facedown, facedown, all the way down," a deputy said during the arrest. The sheriff said the suspects were identified as 29-year-old Ferdinand Schoedinger IV of New Hampshire and 33-year-old James Bolon of Ohio. Both men were reportedly placed at Local Lanes Duckpin Bowling and Eatery on Hutchinson Island. The sheriff said one of the suspects admitted they broke into the business because they wanted to play video games after it had closed. "They had been there earlier, had enjoyed it, were trying to come back and continue playing Pac-Man. And ended up in a serious game of hide-and-go-seek with the Martin County Sheriff's Office," Budensiek said. Budensiek also issued a warning to visitors. "Don't come here and do stupid things; definitely don't come here and try to victimize our citizens," he said. Both suspects have bonded out but face felony burglary charges. A Port St. Lucie family says it has spent nearly four years trying to get a swale liner installed to keep stagnant water from lingering in its yard, a problem the family says leaves water sitting for days and turns the property into what they jokingly call a "mosquito hotel."Oprah Fasulo and her mother, Divika Todd, brought the problem to WPTV's Michael Hoffman after meeting him at WPTV's Let's Hear It community meetup in Jensen Beach.Their frustration centers on a yearslong wait and changing rules over who is responsible for installing the swale liner. Now, the city says the family is not alone and that it recently received approval to add a contractor to help speed up installations.Fasulo and Todd told Hoffman their problem dates back to when their Port St. Lucie home was built.At the time, the city was changing its rules surrounding responsibility for installing swale liners, which are designed to help keep water moving rather than allowing it to remain on properties.According to the family, installation had been the city's responsibility before shifting to builders. It has since shifted back to the city.Their house, they said, was built between those changes and never received one.The family eventually contacted Port St. Lucie."They said that they have to install it. The homeowners are not allowed to install it," Fasulo said.Fasulo said she understood that requirement. What frustrated her was how long her family was told it would take."I understand that totally, but they told us that it was three years; it would be done," she said.Now, Fasulo said the family has been told it could take another two years.That's when they turned to WPTV."We've seen you guys get results," Fasulo told Hoffman.The family provided WPTV with pictures showing water collecting around the property even after lighter rainfall.They also walked Hoffman around their property to show him the problem firsthand.The standing water wasn't the only issue they encountered. Mosquitoes quickly made their presence known.Fasulo has a name for it."Mosquito hotel," she said.For the family, however, the nickname highlights a problem they've been trying to resolve for years: Water takes days to clear from their property, and they say they cannot install the needed liner themselves.Hoffman brought the family's concerns to the city and sat down with Scott Samples to ask why the process has taken so long and what is being done about it.Samples said the family is not the only one waiting."We were recently approved to add a contractor to help us to expedite getting some of these put in," Samples said.The city is also evaluating how to use its available resources to address the outstanding installations more quickly, Samples told WPTV."We're looking at, again, how can we maximize the resources that we have available to help the residents as quickly as we can, knowing that we're limited," Samples said. "You know, so we try to put this, there's plans, and then you have to adjust those plans as you go as well. So we're sort of in that process right now."For Fasulo and Todd, that still does not provide a date for when their swale liner will finally be installed.But after nearly four years of waiting, they now have WPTV asking those questions alongside them."You guys have helped in the past with this issue," Fasulo said. "So we decided to ask you guys to help us and whoever else is in need and not getting answers from the city."WPTV will continue following the family's case and pressing Port St. Lucie for updates on when the work will be completed.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. As if record rainfall wasn’t enough, severe storms Saturday night raced through our area from Palm Beach County through the Treasure Coast.A number of viewers reached out to us from the Bridges community in Delray Beach located off Lyons Road south of Atlantic Avenue.Christopher Daum told us he was prepping dinner when he heard the tornado warning alert on his phone.“All of a sudden it got super windy, super loud. My wife asked me to turn the water off, what was that noise. We looked in the back and saw trees blowing everywhere,” said Daum.There have been no reports of any major injuries as of 9 p.m. Saturday.Viewers sent us video of sheriff’s deputies blocking roads where trees had fallen in the Huntington Lakes community.You can send us your photos to newstips@wptv.com

Saturday evening's severe weather produced a confirmed EF-1 tornado in southern Palm Beach County that had estimated peak winds of 102 mph, according to the National Weather Service.WATCH: NWS confirms Saturday evening tornado in Palm Beach CountyThe National Weather Service began tracking a rotating thunderstorm near Boca Raton before issuing updates as the storm moved toward Delray Beach.At 6:19 p.m. Saturday, the Weather Service confirmed a tornado over Kings Point, moving northeast at 15 mph.The storm prompted tornado warnings across portions of southern and eastern Palm Beach County, with reports of downed trees, damage to homes and power outages. The NWS also issued a tornado watch for Palm Beach County and surrounding areas through 10 p.m. Saturday.After the NWS survey on Sunday, meteorologists confirmed an EF-1 tornado caused the damage. The tornado had peak winds around 102 mph and followed a 7.64-mile path from near Whisper Walk in Boca Raton north to western Boynton Beach near the Westchester Country Club. The width of the storm was 500 yards.No injuries were reported.

The sound of bagpipes and taps filled the air Saturday as the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office unveiled a new memorial honoring two deputies killed in the line of duty.The memorial, located outside the sheriff’s office’s new administration building, honors Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Cpl. Their deaths happened 40 years apart. Now, their names have a permanent place together.WATCH: New memorial honors two Indian River County deputies killed in line of dutyThe unveiling came exactly one year after Sweeting-Mashkow was killed while serving an eviction notice at a home in the Bermuda Club community.47-year-old Sweeting-Mashkow was one of three deputies serving the eviction notice on Nov. 21, 2025, when authorities said 37-year-old Michael Halberstam retrieved a weapon and opened fire. Sweeting-Mashkow was killed, and Deputy Florentino Arizpe was shot in the shoulder.A locksmith who was there for the eviction, David Long, was also critically wounded and later died from his injuries.Sweeting-Mashkow had served with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office for more than 25 years. Her death marked the second line-of-duty death in the 100-year history of the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.For those who gathered Saturday, the passage of a year has not made that loss feel distant.“It’s an honor to be out here but also very sad,” community member Joanne Knott said. “To think that it happened a year ago is strange because it feels like it was yesterday.”The memorial also reaches back four decades, honoring Cpl. Richard Raczkoski, who was killed in the line of duty 40 years ago.“The two heroes that are on this memorial are two people that our community will remember forever,” Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said.Hundreds of family members, friends, law enforcement officers and community members gathered for Saturday’s unveiling, paying their respects.“I am so glad that they did this for Terri and Raczkoski,” one community member said.For those at the ceremony, the memorial is also a reminder of the risks law enforcement officers face each time they go to work.“All of these officers that step out into the community, they never know what their day is going to bring,” says Knott.Flowers hopes the two names on the memorial will be the only ones it ever bears: “I hope we never have to add names to this memorial again."

An EF-1 tornado that touched down in southern Palm Beach County left residents in west Boca Raton and west Delray Beach cleaning up damaged homes, downed trees and crushed vehicles after the storm tore through the area Saturday.The National Weather Service confirmed the tornado touched down along the Kings Point area. WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache spoke with residents who described how quickly conditions changed and how close some came to being caught in the storm.In west Boca Raton, WPTV found a massive uprooted tree that lifted concrete in a parking lot and fell onto three parked vehicles. Video shared with WPTV also showed intense winds as the tornado moved through the area.At Boca Gardens, Thulio Dos Santos, 19, said he was walking home with his brother when he received an alert warning him to take shelter."After that, we started seeing the wind pick up and then the rain started going," Dos Santos said.Dos Santos said he began running for safety as conditions deteriorated. During the storm, a branch struck him in the back of the head.He described the experience as something out of a movie."Honestly, I'm grateful that nothing major happened," Dos Santos said. "I only got hit in the head, but everything is fine."He also expressed relief that there were no deaths in his immediate area.For Alvaro Villa Correa, the storm left behind a different challenge.His vehicle was among those crushed by a fallen tree in west Boca Raton."Honestly, I didn't realize just how powerful and dangerous a tornado could be," Villa Correa told WPTV.He moved to Florida from Venezuela four years ago — unaware of tornado impacts. Villa Correa said he had stepped outside and was heading toward his car when the tornado struck. He did not make it to the vehicle before the tree came down."Fortunately, I didn't have time to make it to my car," he said in Spanish. "It's probably for the best, because I might not be here to tell the story."Villa Correa said the vehicle was his only car and he is still making payments on it. He is now worried about how insurance will handle the loss and how he will get to work.But amid that uncertainty, he said neighbors have already offered to help by giving him rides."I'm scared, surprised and amazed, all three at once," he said.WPTV also documented storm damage at the Gleneagles community in west Delray Beach.For residents accustomed to preparing for hurricanes, the tornado came as a shock.Dos Santos said a tornado hitting so close to home was something he never expected."Crazy, because like 15 seconds did a lot of damage, but when I was there, it felt like a long time," he said.For residents such as Villa Correa, the aftermath now means dealing with damaged property and unexpected expenses while also reflecting on how much worse the tornado could have been.The National Weather Service Miami confirmed the tornado was an EF-1 with estimated peak winds of 102 mph. The tornado traveled about 7.64 miles through southern Palm Beach County, reaching a maximum width of 500 yards, according to a preliminary damage survey released Sunday evening.The National Weather Service said the tornado began around 6:04 p.m. Saturday in the Boca Gardens area and remained on the ground until about 6:31 p.m., eventually lifting as the storm moved over western Boynton Beach.No injuries or fatalities were reported, according to the National Weather Service.Robert Garcia, a warning coordination meteorologist with National Weather Service Miami, was among those who surveyed the tornado damage Sunday.Survey crews found widespread tree damage along the tornado's path, along with occasional roof damage. Damage became more scattered toward the northern end of the surveyed area.According to the National Weather Service, crews were unable to access some gated communities and relied in part on residents to learn about damage in those locations.Meteorologists said the tornado developed after a cell merger and a surge in the storm's rear-flank downdraft allowed its rotating mesocyclone to reach the surface. The tornado eventually weakened and lifted into a visible funnel cloud as it moved over western Boynton Beach.The National Weather Service said its findings are preliminary and could change following a final review of the event.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. About 21,000 customers in Port St. Lucie remain under a precautionary boil water notice after a contractor damaged a water main earlier this week.The city announced it is extending the notice for the Tradition and west Port St. Lucie areas following Tuesday's water main break near Glades Cut Off Road.The notice covers all of Tradition, including Western Grove, Riverland, Wilson Grove and Southern Grove, as well as areas west of Interstate 95 south to Becker Road. Communities along Glades Cut Off Road, including Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano, are also affected.City officials said the notice will remain in place until water quality testing is successfully completed and the city determines it is safe to lift.With an estimated 21,000 customers affected, officials said a significant number of water samples must be collected and tested to ensure the water is safe.The city is asking residents not to tamper with clearly marked hydrants or pipes that are flushing water, warning that interference could delay testing and extend the notice.According to officials, the break was caused by a contractor working on a construction project unrelated to the city. Crews responded and repaired the damaged 36-inch water main within hours before beginning the required flushing process.The city is investigating the incident and expects to pursue appropriate action to recover costs from those responsible.There is no estimated time for when the boil water notice will be lifted.Residents can find updates at CityofPSL.com.

A controversial proposal to build a more than 1.6 million-square-foot data center just half a mile from an elementary school is drawing growing opposition in Martin County, where residents are raising concerns about everything from environmental impacts to whether they'll have a say in the project's approval.WATCH: 'We need answers': Martin Co. officials address outrage over proposed data centerOn Friday morning, a small but vocal group of residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center, demanding answers about the massive development proposed for a parcel of land off Kanner Highway, west of Interstate 95.They had planned to attend a meeting with the county's Growth Management Department. But less than 17 hours before it was scheduled to begin, the county canceled it, citing overwhelming public interest.Residents showed up anyway."We need answers, and we need them quick," said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from nearby Crystal Lake Elementary School. "This story cannot die, or else this is the death of Crystal Lake School."McIntyre, who goes by Coach Mack, became emotional discussing what the proposed development could mean for the school and surrounding neighborhoods."Now that's the death of an A-rated elementary school that I love," he said, his voice breaking.He's far from alone.Residents have raised concerns about potential noise pollution, water consumption, increased electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, declining property values and possible health impacts on children attending Crystal Lake Elementary.Michael Panella, another resident opposing the project, became emotional while explaining why the fight is so personal."It's life. These little ones are innocent," Panella said, referring also to students of Crystal Lake. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site.“They’re probably dropping now because, oh, the data center going there. We don’t want to move there,” Wilson said of property values."We have residences right here, tons of residents. We're all going to have to deal with this."Residents acknowledge they don't yet know for sure what the long-term consequences of the project might be. They don't know whether electricity bills will increase, how much noise the facility could generate or what wildlife habitat might be lost.But they do know that once something of this magnitude is built, there's no easy way to undo it.The controversy intensified Thursday evening when Martin County announced the cancellation of an informal Growth Management meeting scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Friday.At 4:55 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 19, the Martin County Board of County Commissioners posted the following message online:For residents who had planned to attend, the cancellation only added to their frustration."The thing that frustrates me the most about this is the fact that they were willing to do this meeting in private," said resident Alisha Gibbs.Gibbs described herself as "disgusted" and "absolutely appalled" by the situation.But Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden told WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey that the meeting was never intended to be a formal public hearing or a decision-making session.Instead, Walden said, it was an informal meeting requested by members of the public who wanted to ask county staff questions about the development — something his department routinely accommodates for other projects.He said information about the meeting circulated online, creating the impression that county officials were privately considering a decision on the data center.When interest grew beyond what the county could accommodate, officials decided to cancel."We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size," Walden explained. "So we had to cancel, and we'll do some workshops in the future. I believe the applicant is also going to reach out for some public presentations on the subject." When asked why residents weren't being given more opportunities to weigh in, Walden maintained the county has been transparent."We are transparent through the process, and everything can be made available to anyone that is interested," he said.Walden said additional public meetings and workshops will be scheduled to allow residents to ask questions and learn more about the project.But the canceled meeting is only one of several controversies surrounding the development.Another major point of contention is the timing of the developer's application.On Oct. 27, Martin County commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers, temporarily restricting new applications while the county reviews its development regulations.But records show the application for this project was submitted the day before the moratorium was proposed on October 13. That timing means the project is not subject to the temporary restriction, according to county officials.Walden acknowledged the timing but said the county cannot control when developers submit applications."They obviously saw like everybody else that a moratorium was coming, and they got their application in ahead of time," Walden said. "We don't direct applicants ... and we certainly can't pick and choose when these things happen."WPTV reached out to the project applicant and the law firm representing it, requesting comment on the timing of the application and residents' environmental, energy and health concerns.Neither responded by publication time.Perhaps the most significant concern for opponents is whether residents will have any formal say in the project's approval.Under a county ordinance adopted in 2010, during the Great Recession, Martin County established an administrative approval process for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development.Data centers fall within the county's targeted industry classifications. According to Walden, the proposed development is also covered by an existing planned unit development, or PUD, agreement that allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval.That means the project could potentially move forward without a public hearing or recorded vote by county commissioners.For residents demanding a voice in the decision, that distinction is critical.Hussey asked Walden whether there was anything the county could do to give residents more of a say in whether the development is approved."With the moratorium, we'll be looking at our code to make revisions so everything is appropriately reviewed as it comes in," Walden said."To give the public more of a say in future projects?" Hussey asked. "Correct," Walden responded. Residents are also demanding answers about how a development of this size could affect surrounding neighborhoods, wildlife and students at Crystal Lake Elementary School.The proposal initially called for just under 1 million square feet of development. An updated application brings the total to approximately 1.6 million square feet, including an existing warehouse.Among the concerns raised by residents are the potential effects of noise from cooling equipment, increased water and electricity consumption, wildlife habitat loss and possible impacts on nearby property values.Those concerns remain questions, not established consequences of the proposed development.Walden said the county will review the project's potential impacts before making any approval decision.He also emphasized that despite speculation circulating in the community, the data center has not been approved."There is a misconception that this project was already approved — that's very far from the truth," Walden said."This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted."The county says a staff report examining the project is expected to be released in December.Following that report, officials plan to schedule a public forum, likely including a presentation from the applicant, where residents can ask questions and learn more about the development.No date for that meeting has been announced.For opponents, the controversy goes beyond whether a data center belongs on acres of industrial land.It's about who gets to decide what their community becomes — and whether the people who will live with the consequences have a meaningful opportunity to influence that decision.The residents who gathered outside the county building Friday made clear that canceling a meeting would not end their opposition."If they want to actually please the public, they would deny this proposal," Gibbs said.

Residents in Indian River County are dealing with another round of flooding, with approximately 12 roads closed Thursday evening and the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office urging drivers to stay off the roads as water continues to impact neighborhoods.The latest flooding comes just weeks after another round of high water left parts of the Treasure Coast struggling with similar conditions. Residents say this time, however, some neighborhoods appear to have fared better.WATCH: Indian River County residents navigate another round of floodingFor Terry Holly, who moved to the area from Pennsylvania with his wife 23 years ago, the flooding is an unwelcome reminder of what comes with living in Florida.“I escaped the snow to this,” Holly said.Water has surrounded parts of his neighborhood, Vero Lake Estates, leaving some residents with limited ways to get around.“We’re stuck another week. Luckily, we’ve got plenty of groceries and water, so we’re all set,” Holly said.Holly said he and other residents previously dropped their flood insurance policies. But after experiencing repeated flooding, he is reconsidering that decision.“We all dropped it. And we haven’t had it since, but now I’m going to rethink it again,” he said.County officials report multiple road closures along Vero Lake Estates. The Sheriff’s Office is urging drivers to avoid unnecessary travel and stay off flooded roads.Holly said he has not seen vehicles become stranded during this latest round of flooding, unlike the previous event. However, he warned that smaller vehicles may struggle to get through standing water.“The trucks and the high vehicles can get through. The small cars, forget it,” he said.Marjorie Hale said she believes this round of flooding has been handled better than the previous one, with more precautions being taken.But she is concerned about drivers who continue traveling too quickly through flooded neighborhoods.“You’ve got a lot of people who just don’t know how to drive in floodwaters,” Hale said.She also worries about the impact waves from passing vehicles can have on nearby homes, particularly older properties.Hale’s neighborhood experienced flooding during the previous round, too. A comparison of conditions outside her home then and now shows how the water has changed.She said drivers should slow down and consider the people living along those flooded streets.Indian River County Public Schools will be closed Friday as flooding continues to affect the area.For some families, the closure means an early start to Thanksgiving break. Hale said her daughter is old enough to stay home while she goes to work.She is also trying to find some humor in the situation.“We get our own private island. That’s what happens when it floods 6 inches of rainfall,” Hale said.Even her dog knows to be cautious around the water.“I let my dog out. He doesn’t wander off because he’s not willing to get in the floodwaters. Smart dog,” she said.While some residents are finding ways to make the best of the situation, Hale recognizes that other families across the Treasure Coast are dealing with more serious flooding and damage to their homes.Her message to the community is simple: look out for one another.“Invite your neighbors to Thanksgiving,” Hale said.She hopes the latest flooding will bring people together, especially those who may need a helping hand.“So let’s join together as a community,” she said.For updated information on Indian River County public road closures, click here.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. For years, when you thought of sports at William T. Dwyer, you thought of football, basketball and baseball.However, for the past two years, Dwyer has been a statewide golf powerhouse, securing back-to-back state championships.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Dwyer captures second straight state golf title"It was really cool; it was really fun. We had an early pretty big lead, and it kind of got closer at the end," said sophomore golfer Matthew Marigliano.With the boys giving up an early lead on the greens, the ship was righted by a stellar freshman, Martin Bustos, who shot an even par in his final round."It was pretty awesome; it was pretty great we had a great team this year, and it was pretty fun," said Bustos.Pretty fun might be an understatement; this season, the team lost only once. Hundreds of Palm Beach County families will have a complete Thanksgiving dinner on the table this year through Extraordinary Charities' Turkey Takeaway in West Palm Beach.Extraordinary Charities Executive Director Christine Raymond said the organization is providing fully prepared Thanksgiving meals to 400 families across Palm Beach County. Every available meal has already been claimed, and the organization has filled its volunteer needs.Now, Raymond said, the final need is financial support from the community.“This Thanksgiving we're feeding 400 families across Palm Beach County with a fully prepared Thanksgiving meal,” Raymond said. “All of those meals have been claimed. We're all good with our volunteers, and now the last remaining piece is to gather some community financial support because it costs us about $50 per family to feed them.”CLICK HERE to donate.What's inside a Turkey Takeaway meal?For the families receiving the meals, Thanksgiving comes with all the familiar favorites.Ashleigh McDonald with Extraordinary Charities said each meal includes green beans, gravy, cranberry sauce, stuffing, mashed potatoes, pumpkin pie, and a fully cooked turkey.The meals are scheduled for pickup Nov. 24 and 25.The organization's registration information also offered families the opportunity to request diapers by size with their meals.A change of plans in the kitchenPreparing hundreds of Thanksgiving dinners requires plenty of work, and this year's weather forced an adjustment.Chef Greg Schiff said rain meant the team couldn't prepare all the turkeys using its smoker as planned. Still, the kitchen crew kept the operation moving.“We're still getting the job done,” Schiff said. “I have great staff over here, supporting staff with Ms. Shiel, great crew, so everything is worthwhile knowing how it's going to feed people.”The work extended beyond the turkeys.Recipes for Success graduate Ronin Nance was helping portion stuffing into 20-ounce containers, repeating the process meal after meal.“Repetition is the key to learning,” Nance said.Giving families more than a mealExtraordinary Charities board member Cassius Johnson said the families being served are neighbors dealing with the pressure of rising costs.For Johnson, putting food on the table gives families an opportunity to continue a Thanksgiving tradition centered on togetherness.“This is our opportunity to give them the food that's around that table so they can continue with an amazing tradition,” Johnson said. “One of my favorite holidays where we can just give gratitude and give thanks and spark of joy among ourselves.”And even members of the board are part of the hands-on effort. Johnson spent part of the preparation working on cranberry sauce.With all 400 meals claimed and volunteer needs filled, Extraordinary Charities says financial contributions are the remaining way for people to support this year's Turkey Takeaway. Raymond said it costs the organization about $50 to provide a Thanksgiving meal for a family.At a time when household budgets can make a holiday meal more difficult to afford, hundreds of Palm Beach County families will still get a chance to gather around a Thanksgiving dinner, thanks to a community effort underway in West Palm Beach.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A historic Vero Beach neighborhood is getting a new life through art, as sculptor Ross Power leads an effort to transform Edgewood into a vibrant community of artists, galleries, studios and public gathering spaces.Known as the "Father of the Vero Beach Art Village," Power is helping turn a once-overlooked neighborhood into a destination for creativity, where artists can live, work and share their talents.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The transformation is already underway, with murals, public art and community projects taking shape. Power says more galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are in the works, bringing new opportunities for artists, residents and visitors.A historic Vero Beach neighborhood becomes a canvasUnder the shade of a century-old lychee tree, Power reads from a poem dedicated to the tree as a dancer performs beneath its branches."A place where you and me can become we," Power said.For the longtime sculptor, the tree represents something bigger: a gathering place where art can bring people together.That vision is unfolding in Edgewood, a neighborhood established in 1916 that was once home to Vero Beach's first public school and first motel, according to the Vero Beach Art Village organization.Over the years, parts of the neighborhood fell into disrepair. But where others saw aging properties and neglected alleyways, Power saw potential."It spoke to me, and I heard I was once great and now I have fallen into disrepair and not respected at all, and I said we're going to change that," Power told WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts during a tour of the neighborhood.Power has spent decades creating art and helping develop artistic communities, including an art center in Miami.Now, he's bringing that experience to Vero Beach, with an entire neighborhood as his canvas.Turning Edgewood's alleyways into works of artOne of Power's biggest ambitions is transforming 11 alleyways throughout Edgewood into colorful destinations filled with murals and public art."I'm taking the alleys which are the ugliest part of the neighborhood and turning them into mural opportunities where the alleys are going to be like unbelievable for people to come and visit," Power said."There's a lack of buildings but there's not a lack of fences."Power sees those fences, walls and underused spaces as opportunities to showcase local artists and create an outdoor art experience.But the effort goes beyond beautifying back streets.Special zoning allows artists to live and work in the villageThe city of Vero Beach has established Cultural Arts Village zoning districts designed to encourage artistic businesses while preserving Edgewood's historic residential character.According to the city and the Vero Beach Art Village organization, the zoning creates opportunities for art galleries, studios, live-work spaces and other businesses, depending on the property's classification and applicable approvals.The goal is to create a walkable neighborhood where historic homes can become studios and galleries, and artists can collaborate with their neighbors.“I’ve been working on a bunch of different paintings. And we have projects; there's a bunch of different projects we’ve been working on whether it’s for the city or for trying to save big blue, or our community garden, “ said Linwood Addison Fuller IV, an artist who moved to Edgewood for the focus on art. His wife is also an artist.“It’s so much better to be an artist in a community with other artists,” said sculptor Andrew Draminski. “I’m sitting here working and my neighbors are walking their dog down the alley and come on in and we have a cup of coffee or something like that.”The village's vision extends beyond traditional galleries. Organizers hope to create spaces for music, dance, poetry, photography, workshops and other community events.More galleries, studios and community spaces plannedAccording to the nonprofit Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village, the neighborhood's transformation is a grassroots effort involving artists, residents, businesses and volunteers.The organization highlights ongoing initiatives involving murals, public art, studios, galleries, streetscape improvements and community events.Power says additional galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are also in the works.For him, the goal isn't simply to attract visitors. It's to create a community where artists can thrive together and residents can take pride in their neighborhood."If you want to eat great food, hear great music, see great things, meet great artists, this is the place," Power said.And beneath the sprawling branches of that century-old lychee tree, Power hopes the community he's helping cultivate will continue to grow.Where is the Vero Beach Art Village?The Vero Beach Art Village is located in the historic Edgewood neighborhood, just west of downtown Vero Beach.The neighborhood generally stretches between 14th and 20th avenues and 18th and 20th streets.The Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village nonprofit encourages residents and visitors to support the effort through volunteering, donations and participation in community art projects.Click here for more information about the village, its projects and opportunities to get involved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. More than 50 local nonprofits are coming together for the third annual Festival of Giving at the Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast, filling the Jensen Beach museum with holiday displays while allowing community organizations to share the work they do throughout the region. Christina McIntosh, community outreach and events coordinator for the Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast, said participating nonprofits come from communities stretching from Palm Beach County north through the Treasure Coast. “Those are the five counties that our education department here at the museum works with and works with the schools,” McIntosh said. More than Christmas decorations The Festival of Giving uses decorated Christmas trees and holiday displays to introduce visitors to nonprofit organizations serving South Florida and the Treasure Coast. For the organizations involved, the gathering also provides a chance to learn more about one another. Treasure Coast Community Singers is among the nonprofits participating. “The really great thing about this event is that we get to know other nonprofits,” Sharon Savageaux of Treasure Coast Community Singers said. “We get to understand what they do. And we can help spread their word.” The singers also performed at the museum during a festival breakfast event. A Grinch-themed tree with a community mission The GFWC Hobe Sound Woman’s Club is also participating, decorating its display with a Grinch theme. Sandy Vucik, who represented the organization at the festival, said the money it raises supports several community organizations, including Family Promise, CareBag and Real Life Children’s Ranch in Okeechobee. Vucik said the club is currently helping 19 children at the ranch. “We’re really hoping to give them a nice Christmas,” Vucik said. The holiday setting gives visitors a chance to discover organizations they may not otherwise encounter while allowing nonprofits themselves to make new community connections. The festival includes several special events beyond its nonprofit displays. “Santa’s coming into town,” McIntosh said. “He loves this event, so the kids will be able to visit with him.” Family Night is scheduled for Tuesday evening on Nov. 17, at the Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast. An adult holiday pajama party follows Friday The celebration takes a turn for the grown-ups Friday with an adult holiday pajama party. “We will be a museum full of adults dressed in their holiday pajamas because who doesn’t want to go to a party and go home and go right to bed,” McIntosh said. The festival continues through Saturday, Nov. 21, at 2 p.m., according to McIntosh. The Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast is located at 1707 NE Indian River Drive in Jensen Beach.
