A pedestrian was killed Sunday morning in an incident involving a freight train at the Seaway Drive railroad crossing in Fort Pierce, authorities said. The incident was reported at about 7:16 a.m. Nov. 22. The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said it was assisting the Fort Pierce Police Department, the lead agency investigating. A southbound freight train about 2 miles long was stopped, blocking Seaway Drive and affecting crossings at Avenue H, Old Dixie Highway and Chamberlain Boulevard. Motorists traveling to or from the Seaway Drive Bridge were advised to use the Avenue C or Citrus Avenue bridges as alternate routes and avoid the affected crossings. Fort Pierce police will release additional information about the investigation.

Cars were still getting through when CBS12 News reached one of the spots Port St. Lucie police had flagged for high water Thursday. Water pooled along Port St. Lucie Boulevard, and nearby driveways were dry. Earlier, water had made a lane impassable in two places on Village Parkway, and crews were pumping it off Tradition Parkway. Two weeks ago, floodwater stranded drivers across the city. Near Oak Hammock K 8, video showed a mother and daughter wading through chest-deep water. One location in Port St. Lucie recorded 16.7 inches of rain over 60 hours during that storm. Where police reported flooding Port St. Lucie Boulevard: Crews were putting up barricades at McCorkle Avenue, at Alcantara Boulevard and along the stretch from Southwest Liberty Drive to Firestone. Northbound Village Parkway: The right lane was impassable south of the fire station and south of Discovery Way. Water was spreading into a second lane near Discovery Way. Tradition Parkway east of Hazel Drive: Crews were pumping water off the road after the outside lanes flooded in both directions. Police said more closures could be needed as rain continued. The Florida Department of Transportation also had overnight closures scheduled this week on Port St. Lucie Boulevard between Southwest Fisherman and Southwest Liberty avenues for drainage work tied to a widening project. Where to fill sandbags St. Lucie County says sand is still available while supplies last at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds’ west parking lot, 15601 W. Midway Road in Fort Pierce. The Lawnwood Stadium site has run out. The fairgrounds site is self-service. Bring a shovel and plan to fill your own bags. The county has a limited supply of bags and encourages residents to bring their own. Residents in unincorporated St. Lucie County can report flooding that threatens homes, businesses or personal safety to flooding@stlucieco.gov. What was different this time Port St. Lucie crews started lowering water levels in stormwater basins Sunday to make room for more rain. They also cleared drains and checked canals and culverts. A lot of it just depends on how much rain you get at a given time, city spokesperson Scott Samples said. During the Nov. 1 3 storm, Samples said, rain came down so quickly that the drainage system needed longer to move it. This week, he said, less rain had fallen all at once. We’ve been fortunate that so far we haven’t had that kind of rain, he said. Samples said homeowners associations and community development districts manage drainage in parts of Tradition. The city helped pump water out of a neighborhood there after the first storm, he said. It’s really a very collective stormwater system. A flood watch remains in effect for St. Lucie County through 7 p.m. Friday. The National Weather Service issued a separate advisory Thursday morning after radar and gauges indicated 2 to 4 inches had fallen across parts of northeastern St. Lucie County and eastern Indian River County. forecast.weather.gov See also: Who’s responsible for improving drainage after St. Lucie County’s historic flooding? St. Lucie schools reopen St. Lucie Public Schools reopened on a regular schedule Thursday after closing Wednesday over flooding concerns. Aftercare, sports and other activities were scheduled to resume. The district said weather-related absences would be excused with a note from a parent or guardian. In neighboring Indian River County, public schools and district offices were closed Thursday. More rain on already-soaked ground A flood watch covers St. Lucie County through 7 p.m. Friday. The National Weather Service issued a separate advisory Thursday morning for northeastern St. Lucie County and eastern Indian River County after radar and gauges indicated 2 to 4 inches had already fallen across that area. During the Nov. 1 3 storm, one location in Port St. Lucie recorded 16.7 inches of rain over 60 hours. By Nov. 12, St. Lucie County had received at least 472 preliminary reports of property damage from that storm. The county is accepting damage reports from the earlier storm through Nov. 30.

The historic flooding that hit St. Lucie County in early November left hundreds of homes damaged and raised questions about whether the region’s drainage system can handle another major storm. Those concerns are growing as more heavy rain moves through the area this week. The CBS12 News I-Team looked at who oversees the system and what officials say needs to improve. South Florida’s drainage system is a network of canals, ponds, and locks overseen by multiple agencies. In St. Lucie County, responsibilities are shared by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the South Florida Water Management District, the county, cities, local water-control districts, and homeowners’ associations. Who is responsible can depend on the specific canal or drainage system. St. Lucie County Commissioner Cathy Townsend, who has criticized the water management district, said, It was beyond anything any of us could have imagined. More than three days of rain brought over a foot of water to parts of the county, with some areas receiving as much as 17 inches. As water rose, residents called Townsend asking what was being done. They were asking what’s being done. And unfortunately, there wasn’t anything I could tell them except the floodgates are open and the water is flowing, she said. Rain normally drains into ditches and canals and moves toward the St. Lucie River and Indian River Lagoon before flowing out to the ocean. But the heavy rainfall coincided with unusually high tides, limiting the system’s ability to move water out. This was the perfect storm, Townsend said. The king tide, high tide, 20 inches of rain everything was against us. At a water management district meeting days later, board members discussed the condition of the region’s infrastructure. Board member Thomas Hurley called the flooding a wake-up call and said maintaining the system is increasingly important as water levels rise. Board member Jay Steinle said deficiencies in forecasting equipment left the district without enough warning to draw down canals and prepare. I’m surprised that things went as well as they did given we didn’t have any preparation, Steinle said. See also: St. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding; schools closed Wednesday Nyla Pipes, a St. Lucie County resident and water-policy advocate, told the board that warnings had been raised before the flooding. I happened to know that those alarm bells had sounded some weeks before, but many for the past several years, she said. The flooding also exposed vulnerabilities in newer, master-planned communities such as Tradition. In the Vitalia neighborhood, floodwaters covered streets, stranded vehicles, and left some residents without power for days. One possible factor is how the community was built: Tradition relied on the existing canal system, and developers were not required to build a new canal, according to the reporting in the CBS12 News I-Team’s investigation. Townsend said the county needs to do more to maintain its canals and ditches. She also believes the water management district took too long to open one of the canals. She later learned the delay was related to an environmental concern. In my opinion, I do think that the 23 canals could have been opened a lot earlier, she said. Townsend said it is unclear whether opening the canals sooner would have prevented the flooding, given the amount of water the system could take. CBS12 News reached out to the South Florida Water Management District for comment and will update this story when it responds. The flooding also raised insurance concerns. Many of the flooded areas were outside FEMA’s high-risk flood zones, where flood insurance is generally required for federally backed mortgages. Some homeowners in those areas may not have had flood insurance to help cover the damage.

St. Lucie County schools and district offices are closed Wednesday as families prepare for more heavy rain, two weeks after flooding left roads underwater and damaged homes. All aftercare programs, after-school activities and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled. See also: Flood risk continues for the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches through Friday evening The school district said forecasts show the potential for significant rainfall and localized flooding. With the ground already saturated, the district said closing schools was the cautious choice for students, families and employees. Officials are monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures and access to schools, bus stops and transportation routes. The district plans to announce Wednesday evening whether schools will reopen Thursday. Across the Treasure Coast, some residents are filling sandbags to protect their homes. Others are stocking up on groceries and preparing to stay home if roads flood again. Leo Vargas of Port St. Lucie says floodwater rose to his knees two weeks ago, damaging his garage and guitars. He filled sandbags at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds and is adding more around his home. We had a lot of water go into the garage and we just got over the fact that it stopped smelling like mold in there, Vargas said. And then here we go again with this inclement weather. St. Lucie County set up self-service sand distribution sites at the county fairgrounds in Fort Pierce and the Lawnwood Stadium parking lot. Residents need to bring their own bags and shovels and fill the bags themselves. Sand is available while supplies last. By 6 p.m. Tuesday, the two truckloads at Lawnwood Stadium were nearly gone. Glen Ferlance was out for a morning walk Wednesday morning when he spoke with CBS12. He said the flooding two weeks ago kept him from reaching his children. I could not get to cross over to go and see my kids, Ferlance said. I had to park in the um the plaza here and just look on. Ferlance said he lives in Port St. Lucie and he’s preparing for more rain, but hopes the flooding won’t be as severe this time. I just hope that is not too bad like last time. Yes, I’m prepared, he said. I’m going to get something to eat, and I’m running back home in my bed to watch TV and relax until all this is over. He also said he’s glad St. Lucie County schools are closed. I just thank God they’re not school today, so the kids then should be more safe at home, he said. Some residents are also stocking up on food and supplies. Shoppers told CBS12 they’re preparing to stay home if roads flood again. The district said updates about school operations will be shared on its website and social media channels. Martin County canceled after-school activities. Schools in Indian River and Okeechobee counties remain open as of Wednesday morning. Palm Beach County schools and offices are open Wednesday, but the district canceled all after-school activities and athletics because of the afternoon forecast. Aftercare families must pick up their children by 4 p.m., the district said.

A fatal train-versus-pedestrian incident is under investigation Sunday morning at the Seaway Drive railroad crossing, prompting road closures and traffic disruptions across portions of Fort Pierce. According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, the incident was reported around 7:16 a.m. Deputies are assisting the Fort Pierce Police Department, which is leading the investigation. Authorities said a southbound freight train involved in the incident remains stopped at the crossing. The train, estimated to be approximately two miles long, is blocking access at Seaway Drive and affecting traffic at several nearby railroad crossings, including Avenue H, Old Dixie Highway and Chamberlain Boulevard. The closures are impacting travel to and from the Seaway Drive Bridge. Officials are directing drivers to use Avenue C or the Citrus Avenue Bridge as alternate routes. Motorists are encouraged to avoid the area and expect delays while investigators remain on scene. No information about the victim has been released. The Fort Pierce Police Department is continuing its investigation and is expected to provide additional details as they become available.

St. Lucie County residents are preparing for heavy rainfall this week, with officials offering free self-serve sandbag stations and working to clear drainage systems to address potential flooding. Dreamland Park in Fort Pierce, residents were seen filling sandbags to protect their homes. Resident Lisa Powell is concerned. "My ditches are full from the last storm, they haven't gone down, so this could be very bad. The water is just still standing there, up to the yard." Another resident shared their concerns, saying, "My crawlspace got a foot of water in there, so trying to get all these bags to try and cover up the opening, you know." Public works crews in St. Lucie County are actively checking and clearing swales and drainage systems as the area braces for more severe weather. Recent flooding left parts of the county submerged, with residents in the Creekside development trapped inside, some using kayaks to navigate flooded streets while others waded through the water. Fredrick Reeves, a resident whose home was previously flooded, is preparing for the upcoming rain by using sandbags and mulch to block water from entering his house. "It was pretty bad, and the house itself, once it started coming in, I thought maybe we would be alright. I threw down all my clothes trying to soak it up, but that didn't do anything. The next thing you knew, it was in the house," Reeves said. He described the situation as "overwhelming." The City of Fort Pierce is offering free self-serve sandbag stations at Martin Luther King Jr. Dreamland Park and Jaycee Park. Residents are advised to bring their own bags and shovels. Both parks are open daily from dawn to dusk. St. Lucie County has also set up self-service sandbag distribution points at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds West Parking Lot and Lawnwood Stadium Parking Lot, thanks to donations of sand from Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials. Residents must bring their own supplies and fill their own bags. For updates about the precautions residents should take, please visit St. Lucie County’s emergency management portal at: www.readystlucie.org. For more information, residents can contact the Public Works Department or visit the county’s emergency management portal. hero.headline: Flood watch issued for Wednesday as Treasure Coast rain chances increase
hero.body:
A flood watch has been issued for Wednesday, when rain chances on the Treasure Coast are forecast to reach their highest level of the week. Scattered to numerous showers and isolated thunderstorms are possible.

Rain chances are expected to increase slightly Tuesday, with warmer temperatures on the way. The early-week forecast called for a mix of sun and clouds, highs in the mid to upper 70s and light northwest winds.

Partly cloudy skies and light northwest winds were forecast overnight, with lows in the low 60s along the Treasure Coast and in Okeechobee County. Palm Beach County’s overnight lows were forecast in the low to mid 60s.
hero.article_text: Flood Watch issued for Wednesday Flood Watch issued for Wednesday A mix of sun and clouds today, with high temperatures in the mid to upper 70s and light winds out of the northwest. Tonight, partly cloudy skies and light winds out of the northwest. Low temperatures in the low 60s along the Treasure Coast and in Okeechobee County, and low to mid 60s in Palm Beach County. Chances for rain increase a little bit on Tuesday, with warmer temperatures on the way, but the highest rain chances this week will be on Wednesday, with scattered to numerous showers and isolated thunderstorms possible. Stay with WPBF 25 on-air and online for updates. Interactive radar Severe Weather Alerts Download the WPBF 25 News app for the most up-to-date weather alerts.

hero.headline: Two injured in U.S. 1 tractor-trailer crash in Hobe Sound; one flown to hospital
hero.body:
Two people were injured Monday in a crash involving a vehicle and a tractor-trailer at U.S. 1 and SE Hobe Terrace in Hobe Sound, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office.

One person suffered life-threatening injuries and was flown to St. Mary’s Medical Center by Martin County Fire Rescue’s LifeStar, the Sheriff’s Office said. A second person was also injured in the crash.

The Martin County Sheriff’s Office and Florida Highway Patrol are investigating the crash, which the Sheriff’s Office described as a serious injury crash.

hero.headline: Indian River County Sheriff’s Office unveils memorial to two deputies killed in line of duty
hero.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office unveiled a stone memorial Saturday honoring its two deputies killed in the line of duty, dedicating it on the first anniversary of Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow’s death. The roughly 10-foot obelisk bears her name and that of Cpl. Richard Raczkoski outside the agency’s new administration building in Vero Beach.

Hundreds of family members, fellow officers and community members attended the ceremony, which included bagpipes, taps, a three-volley salute, “Amazing Grace,” a rose tribute and the last radio call for Sweeting-Mashkow. The monument stands on the sheriff’s campus at 4055 41st Ave. The administration building is expected to open next spring.

“By placing the memorial at the front of our new administration building before we take occupancy, we ensure that every employee, every visitor, and future generations will always know the names and memory of our fallen heroes,” Sheriff Eric Flowers said. He said he hopes the agency never has to add another name.

Sweeting-Mashkow, 47, was fatally shot while serving an eviction notice at a home in the Bermuda Club community. She had served more than 25 years with the sheriff’s office, much of that time in patrol before moving to the civil process unit. Her death was the second line-of-duty killing in the agency’s roughly 100-year history.

Authorities said Sweeting-Mashkow was one of three deputies at the residence when Michael Halberstam, 37, opened fire. Deputy Florentino Arizpe was shot in the shoulder. Locksmith David Long, who was assisting with the eviction, was critically wounded and later died. Deputies returned fire, and Halberstam died the following day.

Raczkoski, 29, was killed Sept. 23, 1986, after answering a 911 hang-up from a phone booth outside a Zippy Mart on State Road 60 west of Vero Beach. During the encounter, a handgun fell from William Reaves’ clothing. After a short struggle, Reaves shot Raczkoski four times in the back as the deputy tried to run. Reaves was convicted of first-degree murder, sentenced to death and executed Oct. 20, 2026.

hero.headline: Two face felony burglary charges in Hutchinson Island game-room break-in
hero.body:
Two men are facing felony burglary charges after authorities accused them of entering a Hutchinson Island business after closing because they wanted to keep playing video games, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Sheriff John Budensiek identified the suspects as Ferdinand Schoedinger IV, 29, of New Hampshire, and James Bolon, 33, of Ohio. The incident happened late Saturday into early Sunday at the Indian River Plantation Shopping Plaza. Authorities identified the business as Local Lanes Duckpin Bowling and Eatery, which includes a restaurant, bowling alley and game room. Both men have since bonded out.

The investigation began after a security guard patrolling the property noticed something unusual and called 911. According to Budensiek, the guard came across a man at the business's back door. When the guard tried to confront him, the man ran away. The sheriff described that encounter as the initial discovery of the alleged break-in. Video from the sheriff's Air One unit showed deputies following a suspect from the air as officers searched on the ground. In the footage, a deputy directed officers toward the suspect, telling them he would be on their right and instructing them to stop their vehicle.

Deputies found one man walking along the road and another coming out of the woods with an electric scooter, according to the sheriff's account. Footage of the arrest included a deputy ordering a suspect to lie facedown on the ground. Budensiek said one of the men admitted that they had broken into the business to play video games after it had closed. According to the sheriff, the men had visited earlier and wanted to return to continue playing. That explanation, Budensiek said, was the reason one suspect gave for entering the closed business.

“They had been there earlier, had enjoyed it, were trying to come back and continue playing Pac-Man. And ended up in a serious game of hide-and-go-seek with the Martin County Sheriff's Office,” Budensiek said. His account connected the men's earlier visit and desire to play more games with the alleged burglary and the search that followed the security guard's call. The sheriff also delivered a warning to people visiting the area: “Don't come here and do stupid things; definitely don't come here and try to victimize our citizens,” he said. Schoedinger and Bolon both face felony burglary charges despite having bonded out.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County to consider Port of Fort Pierce master plan Dec. 1
hero.body:
St. Lucie County commissioners are scheduled to consider adopting the final draft of the 2026 Port of Fort Pierce Master Plan on Dec. 1, setting a long-term vision for waterfront development and helping the county seek state and federal grants for port improvements. The meeting begins at 6 p.m. in Fort Pierce.

County Port, Inlet and Beaches staff will present the plan. Commissioners can approve the document as presented or amend it before adoption, according to the county. The update supplements the port’s 2020 master plan and incorporates feedback from residents and industry stakeholders since commissioners last reviewed the draft Aug. 11. Its development proposals are part of a long-term vision, while proposed zoning changes and the Port Overlay District remain under discussion.

Among the draft’s long-term opportunities is a Launch Vehicle Recovery Facility to support offshore rocket recovery operations, including drone ships and other support vessels. The proposal is part of a broader mixed-use working waterfront vision that includes mega-yacht services, marine research, workforce training, recreation and public access. The plan calls for continued growth of mega-yacht maintenance and repair operations, along with a marina at Museum Pointe where yachts could dock temporarily for crew changes, provisioning or staging before service.

Harbour Pointe is envisioned as a public-facing district with a regional boat ramp, waterfront dining and commercial space, an entertainment pavilion, a shared-use path and a living shoreline. The update also proposes a marine research and workforce training campus focused on marine science, environmental education and training for waterfront jobs. Infrastructure and access proposals include a new road to Harbour Pointe, stormwater improvements, a possible connection to the regional Sun Trail and a future Port to Park link between the waterfront and Franklin Park.

Commissioners will consider the plan during their regular meeting in the Commission Chambers on the third floor of the Roger Poitras Administration Annex, 2300 Virginia Ave. in Fort Pierce. The meeting will also be streamed on the county’s website and YouTube channel. Residents can review the draft on the county’s Port Master Plan webpage.

hero.headline: Florida agencies could qualify for $1.4 billion in immigration enforcement funds
hero.body:
Florida law enforcement agencies could qualify for up to $1.4 billion in federal immigration enforcement funding through fiscal year 2027, according to new research by fwd.us, a bipartisan immigration and criminal justice advocacy organization. The estimate puts Florida ahead of every other state in potential funding for helping federal authorities enforce immigration laws.

The report estimates fiscal year 2026 funding eligibility at $5.3 million for the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, nearly $1.8 million for Martin County and $880,000 for Indian River County. It also estimates more than $16 million for Palm Beach County and $1.7 million for Okeechobee County. Those figures represent potential funding under the program, rather than payments received.

Since February 2025, Florida has required every law enforcement agency to have a 287(g) agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The agreements authorize state and local officers to perform immigration enforcement activities on ICE's behalf. Felicity Rose, vice president of research and policy at fwd.us, and her team used public and leaked records to estimate funding tied to participation. The report estimates Florida has deputized 9,021 officers under the program's task force model and conducted 15,164 arrests since January 2025.

State arrest figures show a sharp difference between Martin County and nearby counties. Florida Department of Law Enforcement data lists 1,095 arrests under 287(g) for the Martin County Sheriff's Office since August 2025, compared with 361 in Palm Beach County, 38 in Indian River County, 37 in Okeechobee County and 15 in St. Lucie County.

A Martin County Sheriff's Office spokeswoman disputed the figure. She said people without lawful immigration status who are arrested on local criminal charges are booked into the county jail, and those bookings are substantially lower than the state-reported total. She also said the agency had not conducted any recent immigration enforcement operations under 287(g).

ICE's task force payment structure includes an initial $100,000 stipend, plus $7,500 per credentialed officer. Quarterly stipends add $15,000 per officer, alongside salary reimbursement for time spent on immigration enforcement and quarterly performance awards tied to successfully locating people in the country illegally.

Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek supported federal payment for immigration detention assistance in December 2025. “I don't think our taxpayers should be taxed again. I think the federal government, if they're going to use us as a tool, should pay for their portion of that,” Budensiek said.
hero.article_text: New research shows Florida law enforcement agencies could earn more than $1 billion in federal funding through next year for helping the Department of Homeland Security with immigration enforcement operations — far beyond what any other state could receive for its participation.Since February 2025, every law enforcement agency in Florida is required to have a 287(g) agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The agreement allows state and local law enforcement officers to conduct immigration enforcement activities on ICE's behalf. The 287(g) program has been around for 30 years."(It's) basically a program that if someone came into the jail, then the jail could run their information through an immigration database and alert ICE if they had an immigration detainer or some civil immigration issue, and then ICE could come and pick them up," said Felicity Rose, vice president of research and policy at fwd.us, a bipartisan advocacy organization that focuses on immigration and criminal justice. Rose and her team have been tracking the Trump administration's use of 287(g) agreements. They recently published a report using public and leaked records to estimate how much money local law enforcement agencies are getting from ICE in exchange for participating in 287(g)."Those partnerships are both sending billions of dollars to state and local law enforcement with very little oversight," Rose said.I asked Rose for her data on each sheriff's office in our five-county viewing area. In Palm Beach County, the report estimates more than $16 million in available funding for fiscal year 2026. In Martin County, the estimate is nearly $1.8 million, along with $5.3 million in St. Lucie County, $1.7 million in Okeechobee County and $880,000 in Indian River County."After the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act in the summer of 2025 passed, they gave $191 billion to (the U.S. Department of Homeland Security). One thing they decided to do with that was start paying people who signed up for the task force model," Rose explained.ICE breaks down its 287(g) task force payment structure on its website: initial stipends of $100,000, plus $7,500 per credentialed officer. Then, quarterly stipends of $15,000 per officer per quarter. That's on top of salary reimbursement for officers' time working immigration enforcement, plus "quarterly monetary performance awards based on the successful location of illegal aliens.""That money led to a major change in the number of agencies signing up and, very importantly, the number of arrests that they were making," Rose said.The Florida Department of Law Enforcement tracks 287(g) arrests throughout the state. Their data states that since August 2025, the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office had 361, the Okeechobee County Sheriff's Office carried out 37, Indian River County had 38 and St. Lucie County had 15. The Martin County Sheriff's Office had 1,095 287(g) arrests.The Martin County Sheriff's Office declined an interview for this story, but Sheriff John Budensiek spoke to us in December 2025 about accepting funding to help with immigration detention."I don't think our taxpayers should be taxed again. I think the federal government, if they're going to use us as a tool, should pay for their portion of that," Budensiek said.A spokeswoman for MCSO told me in a statement that "The Martin County Sheriff's Office has not conducted any recent immigration enforcement operations under the 287(g) program. Individuals without lawful immigration status who are arrested on local criminal charges in Martin County are booked into the Martin County Jail. The number of those bookings is substantially lower than the figure you cited."Mariana Blanco and her team at the Guatemalan Maya Center in Lake Worth Beach have also been tracking immigration arrests and working with the families impacted by them."When you begin monetizing these arrests, now you lose sight of the protection of the people, and that's exactly what we're seeing," Blanco said.She tells me she's noticed a change in how and where those arrests have happened in recent months in Palm Beach County."So they're not just taking the driver in the vehicle; they're taking the passengers as well," Blanco said."When (people) called to report crimes, (deputies) have been arresting them because of their — due to their immigration status," Blanco said.I asked her if the person who called to report the crime gets arrested, and she confirmed that they do.I asked Blanco whether she worries about the impact that will have on crime overall in Lake Worth."Crime has been heavily under-reported in Lake Worth and I know that because PBSO has asked us for help in ... giving a sense of security for the people to report crimes," Blanco said. "We said, well, respectfully, we don't trust you, and so how would we tell the people that they could trust you?" The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office didn't respond to my requests for comment.The fwd.us report estimates law enforcement agencies across Florida could be eligible for a total of up to $1.4 billion through fiscal year 2027 from the federal government. The report also estimates that Florida has deputized 9,021 law enforcement officers under the 287(g) task force model and conducted 15,164 arrests since January 2025.To compare, the report shows Texas, the state believed to be eligible for the second-highest payday through 287(g), is estimated to qualify for roughly $421 million through FY 2027. The state is estimated to have deputized 4,082 officers and conducted 9,138 arrests through the program (although Rose noted that Florida provides more data on 287(g) than other states).I filed public records requests with our five local sheriff's offices to see how they were spending that money, beyond reimbursement for deputies' time. Those requests are still pending.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

hero.headline: Florida prepares second federal disaster request after renewed flooding
hero.body:
Florida is preparing a second request for a major federal disaster declaration after renewed flooding across the state, Gov. Ron DeSantis said Monday, as flood-response operations continue in Indian River, St. Lucie and other counties. The state’s first request, submitted after flooding earlier this month, is awaiting federal action.

Speaking in Brevard County, DeSantis said the new request would cover a broader area because the latest rainfall affected more counties and communities. Florida Division of Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said damage assessments could be sufficient to move forward as soon as Monday or Tuesday. DeSantis said individual assistance sought in the initial request could help residents with damaged homes, including those without flood insurance, but cautioned that federal aid may cover only part of their losses.

The state has deployed 90 pumps and 22 vacuum trucks during the response in Brevard, Broward, Indian River, Flagler, Palm Beach, St. Lucie and Volusia counties. More than 750 Florida Department of Transportation personnel are working on flood assessments and pumping operations across Central and South Florida, DeSantis said. State agencies have completed nearly 500 floodwater rescues. The Florida National Guard has mobilized 421 personnel, conducted 417 welfare checks and deployed 54 high-water vehicles across six counties.

DeSantis said parts of Cocoa Beach and surrounding communities received 15 to 20 inches of rain in recent days while many were still recovering from earlier flooding. The St. Johns River near Cocoa reached nearly 19 feet Saturday, exceeding the previous record by more than a foot. He warned that the slow-moving river could take weeks or months to fully recede. “There could be more flooding that happens in the near future,” DeSantis said.

Perdue said State Road 50 in Brevard County and State Road 46 in Seminole County remained underwater Monday. He urged people not to drive or walk through floodwater. The state has deployed more than 10,000 feet of temporary flood barriers to protect critical infrastructure, including government buildings and lift stations in Seminole County and HCA Florida Lake Monroe Hospital in Sanford.

A shelter remains open at the Joseph N. Davis Community Center in Melbourne. Four multi-agency resource centers across three counties, including two in Brevard County, have assisted more than 1,600 residents, DeSantis said. The centers will close on Thanksgiving. Residents whose homes are uninhabitable because of flooding can apply for the state’s temporary travel trailer program at emergencyRV.org.

Many of those areas were still recovering from severe flooding earlier this month.WATCH BELOW: Florida seeking more federal aid after historic flooding, according to DeSantisDeSantis said the St. Johns River near Cocoa reached nearly 19 feet on Saturday, surpassing the previous record by more than a foot. "The St. Johns River is a major concern just given how high it has gotten."Florida previously requested a major federal disaster declaration following the first round of flooding earlier this month. hero.headline: Indian River County Sheriff's Office unveils monument to two fallen deputies
hero.teaser: The monument honors Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Deputy Richard Raczkoski. Saturday’s unveiling marked one year since Sweeting-Mashkow was killed during an eviction call near Vero Beach.
hero.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office unveiled a monument Saturday honoring Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Deputy Richard Raczkoski on the first anniversary of Sweeting-Mashkow’s killing. Family, friends, colleagues and community leaders gathered at the sheriff’s office for the unveiling, bringing together the remembrance of two deputies killed nearly 40 years apart.

Sweeting-Mashkow, a 25-year veteran, was shot and killed on November 21, 2025, while responding to an eviction call near Vero Beach. Deputies were serving an eviction notice at a home in the gated Bermuda Club community when investigators say Michael Halberstam opened fire. Deputy Tino Arizpe was wounded, and locksmith David Long was shot and later died at the hospital. Deputies returned fire, and Halberstam died the following day.

“Terri was an amazing deputy. She had a beautiful heart, and she will be missed,” Sheriff Eric Flowers said following her death.

Raczkoski was fatally shot on September 23, 1986, while responding to a call at a Vero Beach convenience store. Investigators said William Reaves shot Raczkoski four times as the deputy tried to flee following a struggle over a gun. Reaves, 77, was executed on October 20, 2026, nearly 40 years after the murder and about a month before the monument’s unveiling.

Both deputies’ names now stand together on the permanent tribute. The sheriff’s office said the monument represents the strength of its law enforcement family and honors those who gave their lives protecting the community.

cards.headline: Washout, damage closed Indian River County roads Friday as flood watch ended
cards.teaser: A washout on 79th Street and damage on 13th Street SW were among the road closures reported Friday. County officials directed drivers to a live closure map for updates.
cards.body:
A roadway washout and other damage closed roads in Indian River County on Friday, even as the National Weather Service canceled the county’s Flood Watch that morning. County officials urged drivers to check road conditions before traveling, allow extra time for detours and never drive through flooded roads.

A washout closed 79th Street west of 130th Avenue, while roadway damage closed 13th Street SW east of 66th Avenue SW. The county also listed 130th Street as closed Friday. In Vero Lake Estates, 104th Avenue was closed between 87th and 93rd streets, as was 83rd Street between 91st and 93rd avenues.

Other roads had partial blockages. Those locations included U.S. 1 near Barber Street, 82nd Avenue at the entrance to Heritage Plantation and Skyline Drive from Periwinkle to Barber Street. Flooding and partial blockages also affected several locations along Old Dixie Highway SW.

The county said its list covered selected locations and directed drivers to its live road closure map for additional closures and updates. Officials said water needed time to recede and damaged roads required assessment and repairs before they could safely reopen. Crews were working in affected areas, and officials asked drivers to give them room and follow barricades.

Additional showers remained possible Friday, though the heaviest rainfall threat was farther north, according to Indian River County Emergency Services. The county said the Indian River County Fairgrounds could be used in the coming days to support emergency management missions for communities to the north facing a greater threat of heavy rain and flooding.

Friday’s closures also included the School District of Indian River County, Marian Fell Library and the Veterans Services office in Sebastian. The Indian River County Shooting Range, Gifford Aquatic Center and North County Aquatic Center were open Friday.

hero.headline: Fatal train-pedestrian incident at Seaway Drive disrupts Fort Pierce crossings
hero.body:
A fatal train-pedestrian incident at the Seaway Drive railroad crossing in Fort Pierce prompted road closures Sunday morning and remains under investigation. The incident was reported around 7:16 a.m. The Fort Pierce Police Department is leading the investigation, with deputies assisting.

Authorities said the southbound freight train remains stopped at the crossing. Estimated to be about two miles long, it is blocking access at Seaway Drive and affecting traffic at nearby railroad crossings, including Avenue H, Old Dixie Highway and Chamberlain Boulevard.

The closures are disrupting travel to and from the Seaway Drive Bridge. Officials are directing drivers to Avenue C or the Citrus Avenue Bridge as alternate routes and urging motorists to avoid the area and expect delays while investigators remain on scene.

hero.headline: Martin County's Kanner Highway data center could get approval without public hearing
hero.body:
A proposed data center off Kanner Highway in Martin County could receive administrative approval without a public hearing or county commission vote under existing development rules, county officials say. The project, which has drawn resident opposition, remains under review. A staff report is expected in December, followed by a public forum where residents can ask questions about the development west of Interstate 95.

Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden said the project is covered by an existing planned unit development agreement that allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval. A county ordinance adopted in 2010 established that process for certain industries to encourage economic development, and data centers fall within those classifications. County officials also say the application was submitted before a one-year moratorium on data centers was proposed, making this project exempt from the temporary restriction. Walden said the county will examine its code during the moratorium to consider revisions affecting review of future projects.

Residents gathered Friday outside the Martin County Administrative Center after the county canceled an informal Growth Management Department meeting less than 17 hours before its scheduled start, citing overwhelming public interest. Walden said members of the public had requested the meeting to ask staff questions, and it was intended as an informal discussion rather than a decision-making session. He said interest grew beyond the space the county could accommodate. The county has promised public meetings and workshops. “We need answers, and we need them quick,” said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from nearby Crystal Lake Elementary School.

The updated application calls for approximately 1.6 million square feet of development, including an existing warehouse, compared with an initial proposal of just under 1 million square feet. The proposed data center would be half a mile from Crystal Lake Elementary School. Residents have raised concerns about noise from cooling equipment, water and electricity consumption, wildlife habitat, property values and possible health effects on students. Walden said the county will review potential impacts before deciding on approval. “This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted.” Officials plan to schedule the public forum after the December staff report, likely with a presentation from the applicant.
hero.article_text: A controversial proposal to build a more than 1.6 million-square-foot data center just half a mile from an elementary school is drawing growing opposition in Martin County, where residents are raising concerns about everything from environmental impacts to whether they'll have a say in the project's approval. WATCH: 'We need answers': Martin Co. officials address outrage over proposed data center On Friday morning, a small but vocal group of residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center, demanding answers about the massive development proposed for a parcel of land off Kanner Highway, west of Interstate 95. They had planned to attend a meeting with the county's Growth Management Department. But less than 17 hours before it was scheduled to begin, the county canceled it, citing overwhelming public interest. Residents showed up anyway. "We need answers, and we need them quick," said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from nearby Crystal Lake Elementary School. "This story cannot die, or else this is the death of Crystal Lake School." McIntyre, who goes by Coach Mack, became emotional discussing what the proposed development could mean for the school and surrounding neighborhoods. "Now that's the death of an A-rated elementary school that I love," he said, his voice breaking. Residents have raised concerns about potential noise pollution, water consumption, increased electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, declining property values and possible health impacts on children attending Crystal Lake Elementary. Michael Panella, another resident opposing the project, became emotional while explaining why the fight is so personal. These little ones are innocent," Panella said, referring also to students of Crystal Lake. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site. “They’re probably dropping now because, oh, the data center going there. We don’t want to move there,” Wilson said of property values. "We have residences right here, tons of residents. We're all going to have to deal with this." Residents acknowledge they don't yet know for sure what the long-term consequences of the project might be. They don't know whether electricity bills will increase, how much noise the facility could generate or what wildlife habitat might be lost. But they do know that once something of this magnitude is built, there's no easy way to undo it. The controversy intensified Thursday evening when Martin County announced the cancellation of an informal Growth Management meeting scheduled for 9:30 a.m. 19, the Martin County Board of County Commissioners posted the following message online: "This meeting has been canceled. Due to the level of public interest, a more formal meeting will be scheduled and publicly noticed in advance to accommodate any and all residents who wish to attend, learn more, and share their thoughts. Stay tuned to our website and social media as meeting details are finalized." For residents who had planned to attend, the cancellation only added to their frustration. "The thing that frustrates me the most about this is the fact that they were willing to do this meeting in private," said resident Alisha Gibbs. Gibbs described herself as "disgusted" and "absolutely appalled" by the situation. But Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden told WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey that the meeting was never intended to be a formal public hearing or a decision-making session. Instead, Walden said, it was an informal meeting requested by members of the public who wanted to ask county staff questions about the development — something his department routinely accommodates for other projects. He said information about the meeting circulated online, creating the impression that county officials were privately considering a decision on the data center. When interest grew beyond what the county could accommodate, officials decided to cancel. "We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size," Walden explained. "So we had to cancel, and we'll do some workshops in the future. I believe the applicant is also going to reach out for some public presentations on the subject." When asked why residents weren't being given more opportunities to weigh in, Walden maintained the county has been transparent. "We are transparent through the process, and everything can be made available to anyone that is interested," he said. Walden said additional public meetings and workshops will be scheduled to allow residents to ask questions and learn more about the project. But the canceled meeting is only one of several controversies surrounding the development. Another major point of contention is the timing of the developer's application. 27, Martin County commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers, temporarily restricting new applications while the county reviews its development regulations. But records show the application for this project was submitted the day before the moratorium was proposed on October 13. That timing means the project is not subject to the temporary restriction, according to county officials. Walden acknowledged the timing but said the county cannot control when developers submit applications. "They obviously saw like everybody else that a moratorium was coming, and they got their application in ahead of time," Walden said. "We don't direct applicants ... and we certainly can't pick and choose when these things happen." WPTV reached out to the project applicant and the law firm representing it, requesting comment on the timing of the application and residents' environmental, energy and health concerns. Neither responded by publication time. Perhaps the most significant concern for opponents is whether residents will have any formal say in the project's approval. Under a county ordinance adopted in 2010, during the Great Recession, Martin County established an administrative approval process for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development. Data centers fall within the county's targeted industry classifications. According to Walden, the proposed development is also covered by an existing planned unit development, or PUD, agreement that allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval. That means the project could potentially move forward without a public hearing or recorded vote by county commissioners. For residents demanding a voice in the decision, that distinction is critical. Hussey asked Walden whether there was anything the county could do to give residents more of a say in whether the development is approved. "With the moratorium, we'll be looking at our code to make revisions so everything is appropriately reviewed as it comes in," Walden said. "To give the public more of a say in future projects?" Hussey asked. "Correct," Walden responded. Residents are also demanding answers about how a development of this size could affect surrounding neighborhoods, wildlife and students at Crystal Lake Elementary School. The proposal initially called for just under 1 million square feet of development. An updated application brings the total to approximately 1.6 million square feet, including an existing warehouse. Among the concerns raised by residents are the potential effects of noise from cooling equipment, increased water and electricity consumption, wildlife habitat loss and possible impacts on nearby property values. Those concerns remain questions, not established consequences of the proposed development. Walden said the county will review the project's potential impacts before making any approval decision. He also emphasized that despite speculation circulating in the community, the data center has not been approved. "There is a misconception that this project was already approved — that's very far from the truth," Walden said. "This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted." The county says a staff report examining the project is expected to be released in December. Following that report, officials plan to schedule a public forum, likely including a presentation from the applicant, where residents can ask questions and learn more about the development. No date for that meeting has been announced. For opponents, the controversy goes beyond whether a data center belongs on acres of industrial land. It's about who gets to decide what their community becomes — and whether the people who will live with the consequences have a meaningful opportunity to influence that decision. The residents who gathered outside the county building Friday made clear that canceling a meeting would not end their opposition. "If they want to actually please the public, they would deny this proposal," Gibbs said.

cards.headline: Indian River County Sheriff’s Office unveils memorial honoring two fallen deputies
cards.teaser: The permanent memorial honors Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Cpl. Richard Raczkoski. Saturday’s unveiling marked one year since Sweeting-Mashkow was killed while serving an eviction notice in the Bermuda Club community.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office unveiled a permanent memorial Saturday honoring Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Cpl. Richard Raczkoski, whose line-of-duty deaths occurred 40 years apart. The ceremony came exactly one year after Sweeting-Mashkow was killed while serving an eviction notice at a home in the Bermuda Club community.

Hundreds of family members, friends, law enforcement officers and community members gathered outside the sheriff’s office’s new administration building, where the memorial stands. Bagpipes and taps sounded during the ceremony. “The two heroes that are on this memorial are two people that our community will remember forever,” Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said.

Sweeting-Mashkow, 47, was one of three deputies serving the eviction notice on Nov. 21, 2025, when authorities said Michael Halberstam, 37, retrieved a weapon and opened fire. Sweeting-Mashkow was killed, and Deputy Florentino Arizpe was shot in the shoulder. David Long, a locksmith there for the eviction, was critically wounded and later died from his injuries.

Sweeting-Mashkow had served with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office for more than 25 years. Her death was the second line-of-duty death in the agency’s 100-year history. The memorial places her name alongside that of Raczkoski, who was also killed in the line of duty.

For community member Joanne Knott, the anniversary brought a sense of how recent the loss still felt. “It’s an honor to be out here but also very sad,” Knott said. “To think that it happened a year ago is strange because it feels like it was yesterday.”

Knott also reflected on the risks officers face: “All of these officers that step out into the community, they never know what their day is going to bring.” Flowers expressed his hope for the memorial’s future: “I hope we never have to add names to this memorial again.”

cards.headline: Indian River County roads closed Friday despite flood watch cancellation
cards.teaser: A roadway washout and flooding affected roads across Indian River County Friday. County officials directed drivers to a live road closure map for updates before traveling.
cards.body:
Flooding and roadway damage closed several Indian River County roads Friday despite the National Weather Service’s cancellation of the county’s Flood Watch that morning. The county reported a washout on 79th Street west of 130th Avenue and closures in Vero Lake Estates, along with partial blockages on other roads.

The county’s Friday list identified 130th Street as closed. A roadway washout closed 79th Street west of 130th Avenue, while roadway damage closed 13th Street SW east of 66th Avenue SW. In Vero Lake Estates, 104th Avenue was closed between 87th and 93rd streets, and 83rd Street was closed between 91st and 93rd avenues.

Partial blockages affected U.S. 1 near Barber Street, 82nd Avenue at the entrance to Heritage Plantation, and Skyline Drive from Periwinkle to Barber Street. Old Dixie Highway SW had flooding and partial blockages at several locations. The county said its list covered selected locations and directed drivers to the live road closure map for additional closures and updates.

Officials urged drivers to check road conditions before traveling, allow extra time for detours and never drive through flooded roads. Water needs time to recede, and damaged roads must be assessed and repaired before they can safely reopen, officials said. Crews were working in affected areas, and drivers were asked to give them room and follow barricades.

Additional showers remained possible Friday, with the heaviest rainfall threat farther north, according to Indian River County Emergency Services. The School District of Indian River County was closed Friday, as were Marian Fell Library and the Veterans Services office in Sebastian. The Indian River County Shooting Range, Gifford Aquatic Center and North County Aquatic Center were open Friday.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie lifts boil water notice for about 21,000 customers after main break
cards.teaser: Testing confirmed the water was safe in Tradition and western Port St. Lucie. The city is investigating the break and plans to recover costs from the responsible parties.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie lifted its precautionary boil water notice Saturday for the Tradition and western Port St. Lucie area after testing confirmed the water was safe. An estimated 21,000 customers were affected by the disruption following Tuesday’s water main break near Glades Cut Off Road.

The city is investigating the incident and plans to pursue all appropriate actions to recover costs from the responsible parties. A contractor working on a construction project caused the break, according to the city.

City personnel responded immediately and completed repairs to the 36-inch water main by Tuesday evening. On Wednesday, the city announced that water service had been restored for customers west of Interstate 95. The disruption required a significant number of testing samples before the precautionary notice could be lifted.

The city had recommended a 48-hour precautionary boil water notice Tuesday for all of the Tradition area, including Western Grove, Riverland, Wilson Grove and Southern Grove, west of Interstate 95 and south of Becker Road. The notice also covered communities along Glades Cut Off Road, including Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano.

hero.headline: Indian River County unveils monument honoring two fallen deputies
hero.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office unveiled a permanent monument Saturday honoring Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Deputy Richard Raczkoski on the first anniversary of Sweeting-Mashkow's killing. The 25-year veteran was shot and killed while responding to an eviction call near Vero Beach on November 21, 2025.

Family, friends, colleagues and community leaders gathered at the sheriff's office for the unveiling. The agency said the monument represents the strength of its law enforcement family and serves as a reminder that deputies who gave their lives protecting the community will never be forgotten.

Sweeting-Mashkow was serving an eviction notice with other deputies at a home in the gated Bermuda Club community when investigators say Michael Halberstam opened fire. Sweeting-Mashkow was killed, Deputy Tino Arizpe was wounded, and locksmith David Long was shot and later died at the hospital. Deputies returned fire, and Halberstam died the following day.

“Terri was an amazing deputy. She had a beautiful heart, and she will be missed,” Sheriff Eric Flowers said following her death.

Raczkoski was fatally shot on September 23, 1986, while responding to a call at a Vero Beach convenience store. Investigators said William Reaves shot Raczkoski four times as the deputy tried to flee following a struggle over a gun. Reaves, 77, was executed on October 20, 2026, nearly 40 years after the murder and about a month before the monument's unveiling.

hero.headline: Indian River County Sheriff's Office unveils monument honoring two fallen deputies
hero.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office unveiled a monument Saturday honoring Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Deputy Richard Raczkoski on the first anniversary of Sweeting-Mashkow’s killing during an eviction call near Vero Beach. Family, friends, colleagues and community leaders gathered at the sheriff’s office for the unveiling, bringing together the remembrance of two deputies killed nearly 40 years apart.

Sweeting-Mashkow, a 25-year veteran, was shot and killed on November 21, 2025, while deputies were serving an eviction notice at a home in the gated Bermuda Club community. Investigators said Michael Halberstam opened fire, killing Sweeting-Mashkow and wounding Deputy Tino Arizpe. Locksmith David Long also was shot and later died at the hospital. Deputies returned fire, and Halberstam died the following day.

“Terri was an amazing deputy. She had a beautiful heart, and she will be missed,” Sheriff Eric Flowers said following her death.

The monument places both deputies’ names together in a permanent tribute. The sheriff’s office said it represents the strength of its law enforcement family and serves as a reminder of those who gave their lives protecting the community.

hero.headline: Indian River County unveils permanent memorial honoring two fallen deputies
hero.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office unveiled a permanent memorial Saturday honoring Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Cpl. Richard Raczkoski, marking exactly one year since Sweeting-Mashkow was killed while serving an eviction notice in the Bermuda Club community.

Hundreds of family members, friends, law enforcement officers and community members gathered outside the sheriff’s office’s new administration building for the unveiling. Bagpipes and taps sounded during the ceremony honoring the two deputies, whose deaths occurred 40 years apart.

“The two heroes that are on this memorial are two people that our community will remember forever,” Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said.

Sweeting-Mashkow, 47, was one of three deputies serving an eviction notice at a home on Nov. 21, 2025, when authorities said Michael Halberstam, 37, retrieved a weapon and opened fire. Sweeting-Mashkow was killed, and Deputy Florentino Arizpe was shot in the shoulder. David Long, a locksmith who was there for the eviction, was critically wounded and later died from his injuries.

Sweeting-Mashkow had served with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office for more than 25 years. Her death was the second line-of-duty death in the agency’s 100-year history. Raczkoski was killed in the line of duty 40 years ago.

“It’s an honor to be out here but also very sad,” community member Joanne Knott said. “To think that it happened a year ago is strange because it feels like it was yesterday.”

Knott also reflected on the risks officers face at work. “All of these officers that step out into the community, they never know what their day is going to bring,” she said.

Flowers expressed hope that the memorial would bear only the two deputies’ names: “I hope we never have to add names to this memorial again.”

cards.headline: Indian River County flooding closed roads; Friday school closure announced
cards.teaser: About 12 roads were closed Thursday evening as flooding again affected Indian River County. In Vero Lake Estates, residents described limited access and concerns about vehicles pushing water toward homes.
cards.body:
Flooding left approximately 12 roads closed in Indian River County on Thursday evening, and Indian River County Public Schools said schools would be closed Friday. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office urged drivers to avoid unnecessary travel and stay off flooded roads.

County officials reported multiple road closures in Vero Lake Estates, where water surrounded parts of the neighborhood and limited some residents’ routes. The flooding came just weeks after another round of high water affected parts of the Treasure Coast. Some residents said their neighborhoods appeared to have fared better this time.

Terry Holly, who moved to the area from Pennsylvania with his wife 23 years ago, said he had stocked enough food and water to remain home. “We’re stuck another week. Luckily, we’ve got plenty of groceries and water, so we’re all set,” Holly said. He said repeated flooding had also prompted him to reconsider his decision to drop flood insurance.

Holly cautioned that smaller vehicles could struggle in the standing water. “The trucks and the high vehicles can get through. The small cars, forget it,” he said.

Resident Marjorie Hale said she believed the latest flooding had been handled better than the previous round, with more precautions being taken. Still, she expressed concern about motorists driving too quickly through flooded neighborhoods and the waves their vehicles could send toward nearby homes, particularly older properties. “You’ve got a lot of people who just don’t know how to drive in floodwaters,” Hale said. She urged drivers to slow down and consider the people living along those streets.

Hale’s neighborhood also flooded during the earlier round of high water. For her family, the planned school closure meant an early start to Thanksgiving break. She said her daughter was old enough to stay home while she went to work.

Hale acknowledged that other families across the Treasure Coast were facing more serious flooding and damage to their homes. She encouraged residents to support their neighbors during the holiday. “Invite your neighbors to Thanksgiving,” Hale said. “So let’s join together as a community.”

hero.headline: Federal disaster request for Martin County flooding remains pending
hero.body:
Florida Division of Emergency Management Director Jared Perdue confirmed the state submitted an expedited federal disaster declaration request Nov. 9 following the Nov. 2 flooding in Martin County. The request remains pending as the county estimates approximately $18 million in residential and public infrastructure damage. Asked about rebuilding assistance if federal aid is denied, Perdue emphasized coordination with FEMA, nonprofit partnerships and emergency response efforts. A federal major disaster declaration could make certain public repairs eligible for FEMA reimbursement and potentially provide individual assistance to qualifying residents.

In Jensen Beach, dumpsters line driveways along Hyline Drive, where homes have been stripped to their frames and residents have discarded waterlogged belongings. Linda Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters for nine days before beginning to salvage possessions. Weisbecker has been approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program. Martin County is working to distribute approximately $1 million in SHIP funding to qualifying residents. Eligible homeowners may receive grants of up to $25,000, with additional assistance potentially available through loans of up to $75,000. Those loans carry repayment requirements and liens, and income limits restrict eligibility.

Commissioner Blake Capps proposed a separate county-funded emergency assistance program for residents who fall outside existing eligibility requirements. “There's going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where somebody barely missed the limit,” Capps said during a recent Martin County Commission meeting. County Human Services Director Michelle Miller told commissioners the state had promised additional disaster relief funding. When asked about help for families who earn too much to qualify for existing assistance but cannot afford repairs, Perdue pointed to National Guard personnel and nonprofit organizations helping remove damaged drywall and other waterlogged materials from homes to help prevent mold growth.

The county also faces approximately $15 million in combined beach and road damage, while emergency response expenses are still being assessed. County spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess said the county could be responsible for those costs if federal reimbursement is denied, potentially requiring officials to redirect budget money or find other funding sources. Perdue said damage assessments would continue to be submitted to FEMA. The state is also responding to another significant rainfall event, and Ron DeSantis expanded the state's emergency executive order to include 21 counties. Perdue said state resources remain available for immediate needs, including food, water, shelter and emergency medical assistance.
hero.article_text: Nearly three weeks after historic flooding forced families from their homes and caused millions of dollars in damage across Martin County, residents are still waiting for a federal disaster declaration that could unlock critical financial assistance. Now, after a WPTV report on the delays and growing frustration among flood victims, Florida's top emergency management official is responding to questions about the state's recovery efforts—and what help families can expect if FEMA funding never arrives. Watch more from Kate Hussey: In an exclusive interview with WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey, Jared Perdue, director of the Florida Division of Emergency Management, confirmed the state submitted an expedited federal disaster declaration request Nov. 9, one week after the initial flooding. But nearly two weeks after that request, a decision remains pending. "We've been very engaged with FEMA, and we did actually submit an expedited disaster declaration request to FEMA on November the ninth," Perdue said. "FEMA has been very closely coordinating with us in reviewing that, and I'm sure they're going to make quick work of it." The uncertainty comes as Martin County estimates approximately $18 million in residential and public infrastructure damage, with families still struggling to afford repairs and another round of historic rainfall complicating recovery efforts. Along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, the devastation is still visible. Dumpsters line driveways, waterlogged belongings have been discarded and homes have been stripped down to their frames. For Linda Weisbecker, whose home was among those severely damaged, the destruction has been overwhelming. "It's like an apocalypse here," Weisbecker told WPTV in an earlier interview. For nine days, Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters before they could begin salvaging what remained of their homes. "Once we got through that and the water came out, we just all started pitching in, going in to see what we can salvage from each home," she said. But much of what Weisbecker lost cannot be replaced. Our house is empty," she said. "We lost everything, from pictures of our children and their lives, our friends, our grandkids, now we have great-grandkids. Everything [my husband] had since he was 13 on is gone." Weisbecker has been approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program. But for families facing tens of thousands of dollars in repairs, that assistance may cover only a fraction of the cost. And not everyone will qualify. "You do think about that process and you sit there and you say to yourself, how am I gonna do this?" Weisbecker said. That question is at the center of WPTV's ongoing investigation. Martin County estimates the flooding caused: A federal major disaster declaration could make certain public infrastructure repairs eligible for FEMA reimbursement and potentially open the door to individual assistance for qualifying residents. But approval is not guaranteed. When WPTV initially contacted FEMA, the agency confirmed it had received the disaster declaration request and that it remained under review. FEMA referred additional questions about the response and recovery timeline to the Florida Division of Emergency Management. Hussey subsequently pressed Perdue on what would happen if the federal government denied the request. "If FEMA ultimately denies federal assistance, does Florida have a Plan B, or are these families simply on their own?" Hussey asked. Perdue did not identify a specific alternative state funding program, instead emphasizing Florida's experience responding to natural disasters and its ongoing coordination with federal and local officials. "This is something that we're very used to doing. I mean, in Florida, we deal with natural disasters all the time," Perdue said. "We have a great relationship with FEMA, and usually those things go very well." He added that the state remains focused on immediate response efforts, including search and rescue operations and meeting residents' emergency needs. In the meantime, Martin County is working to distribute approximately $1 million in available SHIP funding to qualifying residents. Eligible homeowners may receive grants of up to $25,000, with additional assistance potentially available through loans of up to $75,000. However, those loans come with repayment requirements and liens. Income eligibility restrictions could also leave some families without assistance, even if they cannot afford to rebuild on their own. "There's going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where somebody barely missed the limit," Commissioner Blake Capps said during a recent Martin County Commission meeting. Capps proposed establishing a separate county-funded emergency assistance program for residents who fall through the cracks. But when WPTV asked where that money would come from, Capps acknowledged a funding source had not yet been identified. we'd have to talk to staff," he said. County Human Services Director Michelle Miller previously told commissioners the state had promised additional disaster relief funding, although neither the amount nor the timeline had been confirmed. "They haven't confirmed the amount yet but has assured us we will be getting some disaster relief funds," Miller told Hussey. Hussey raised those concerns directly with Perdue, asking whether the state had other programs available for families who earn too much to qualify for existing assistance but not enough to pay for repairs. Perdue pointed to the state's partnerships with nonprofit organizations and its deployment of emergency personnel to assist with cleanup. "We've actually activated the National Guard, and are also partnering with nonprofits to do what they call the muck and gut of homes that have been flooded," Perdue said. That work includes removing damaged drywall and other waterlogged materials to help prevent mold growth. "We're providing the assistance that we can and partnering with those nonprofit organizations as well," he said. However, Perdue did not identify a specific funding program to cover rebuilding costs for homeowners who do not qualify for existing assistance. The financial uncertainty extends beyond individual homeowners. Martin County faces approximately $15 million in combined beach and road damage, with additional emergency response expenses still being assessed. County spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess previously told WPTV that without federal reimbursement, Martin County could be left responsible for covering those costs, potentially forcing officials to redirect money from elsewhere in the budget or identify other funding sources. Hussey asked Perdue whether the state would help cover those expenses if FEMA denied federal assistance — or whether the financial burden could ultimately fall on local taxpayers. Perdue did not commit to providing state funding for those repairs. "We are and have been doing damage assessments ever since we submitted the first disaster declaration request," he said. "As those damage assessments come in, we'll continue to coordinate with FEMA and make sure all that information is submitted." The state's response follows an emotional Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, where residents pleaded with elected officials to do more to secure recovery funding. Fight for us!" one resident urged commissioners. Others questioned why families were being asked to wait even longer for answers. "And the answer from this dais is wait 13 more days?!?" another resident asked. Commissioner Eileen Vargas said she had reached out to FEMA through personal contacts in an effort to expedite the process. "I did, through contacts, reach out to FEMA to try and get this going," Vargas said. Vargas also told residents she expected a new FEMA director to take office Nov. 30 and hoped that development could help move the disaster declaration forward. But even if a declaration is approved, not all losses or recovery expenses would necessarily qualify for federal assistance. As Martin County continues to recover from the Nov. 2 flooding, Perdue said the state is also responding to another significant rainfall event affecting communities across Florida. Ron DeSantis expanded the state's emergency executive order to include 21 counties. The state has mobilized resources from the National Guard, State Guard, Florida Highway Patrol and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, among other agencies. "We're actively still responding to the previous flooding event on November 2, and now we're actively dealing with a current, another historic rain event that's brought record amount of flooding in many counties throughout the state," Perdue said. The overlapping disasters have added urgency to recovery efforts, particularly for residents whose homes remain exposed after being gutted. Perdue said state resources remain available for immediate needs, including food, water, shelter and emergency medical assistance. We're fully mobilized," he said. We're going to be with you till the very end, and we're going to make sure we help everybody get back on their feet." Despite those assurances, several critical questions remain unresolved. FEMA has not announced a decision on Florida's expedited disaster declaration request. The state has not identified a specific alternative rebuilding assistance program for homeowners who do not qualify for existing aid, nor has it committed to covering Martin County's public infrastructure losses if federal funding is denied. For residents like Weisbecker, the uncertainty is more than a question of government funding. It's a question of whether they can afford to return to the homes they've spent years building their lives in. "This is very urgent for people to get back into their daily lives," Weisbecker said. "This is total devastation.
